text:
An Interlude Between Judgments
Revelation Chapter 14
The Final Harvest of the Earth
Part 8 of 9

John's vision now shifts once again. Having heard the three angelic proclamations—the everlasting Gospel, the announcement of Babylon's fall, and the warning against receiving the mark of the beast—he now witnesses the beginning of God's final harvest of the earth.

"Then I looked, and behold, a white cloud, and on the cloud sat One like the Son of Man, having on His head a golden crown, and in His hand a sharp sickle. And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to Him who sat on the cloud, 'Thrust in Your sickle and reap, for the time has come for You to reap, for the harvest of the earth is ripe.' So He who sat on the cloud thrust in His sickle on the Earth, and the Earth was reaped."
— Revelation 14:14–16

At last, the appointed moment has arrived. The time has come for the Lord Jesus Christ to exercise His authority over the earth and begin reclaiming what is rightfully His. Throughout history, humanity has rebelled against its Creator, rejecting His rule in favor of its own. During the Tribulation, that rebellion reaches its climax under the leadership of the Antichrist. Now, however, the true King steps forward to execute His righteous judgment.

John describes the One seated upon the white cloud as:

"...One like the Son of Man, having on His head a golden crown, and in His hand a sharp sickle."

There is little reason to doubt that this is the Lord Jesus Christ. The title "Son of Man" is one of our Lord's favorite titles for Himself throughout the Gospels and is rooted in Daniel's prophetic vision:

"I was watching in the night visions, And behold, One like the Son of Man, Coming with the clouds of heaven!... Then to Him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom." (Daniel 7:13–14)

Jesus repeatedly identified Himself with this prophecy (Matthew 24:30; 26:64), making it clear that He is the promised Messiah who will one day return in glory to establish His everlasting Kingdom.

Some interpreters have questioned whether the One on the cloud is truly Christ because verse 15 records:

"And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to Him who sat on the cloud..."

From this, they conclude that an angel would never speak in such a manner to the Son of God and therefore suggest that the One on the cloud must be another angel.

The text, however, does not require such a conclusion.

The angel is not issuing a command to Jesus as though exercising authority over Him. Rather, the angel serves as a heavenly messenger announcing that the appointed time established by the Father has arrived. Throughout Scripture, angels frequently communicate God's purposes and declarations without implying superiority over those to whom they speak.

Jesus Himself declared during His earthly ministry:

"But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but My Father only." (Matthew 24:36)

The Father alone determines the appointed hour for the consummation of His redemptive plan. The angel's proclamation therefore serves as Heaven's announcement that the Father's appointed time has come. Far from commanding Christ, the angel joyfully declares that the hour of judgment has arrived.

One might compare this scene to soldiers eagerly awaiting the command of their victorious commander. When the long-anticipated moment arrives, they shout with anticipation, ready to carry out the mission entrusted to them. Their proclamation does not imply equality with their commander but joyful participation in his victory.

Likewise, the angels throughout Revelation function as God's servants and messengers. They announce His decrees, execute His judgments, and faithfully carry out His will. The authority always belongs to God; the angels simply minister in obedience to His command.

John also notes that Christ wears:

"...a golden crown..."

The Greek word used here is stephanos, the victor's crown awarded to one who has conquered in conflict. This differs from the Greek word diadēma, which refers to the royal crown of sovereign authority.

The distinction is significant.

When Jesus came the first time, He wore neither crown of earthly glory nor royal splendor. Instead, Roman soldiers mocked Him by weaving together a cruel crown of thorns and pressing it upon His brow (Matthew 27:29). The King of kings willingly bore humiliation, suffering, and rejection so that sinners might receive forgiveness.

Now John sees that same Savior wearing a victor's crown. The battle has been won. Through His death and resurrection, Christ conquered sin, death, and Satan. His appearance with the stephanos beautifully symbolizes His complete triumph over every enemy.

Later, when Christ returns visibly to the earth upon a white horse, John will describe Him as wearing many diadems (Revelation 19:12), signifying His absolute sovereign authority as King of kings and Lord of lords. Here in Revelation 14, however, the emphasis is upon His victory as the conquering Redeemer whose triumph has secured the final judgment of evil.

Charles H. Spurgeon beautifully captures this contrast:

"How different it will be to see him with a crown of gold upon his head from what it was to see him wearing that terrible crown of thorns which the cruel soldiers plaited, and thrust upon his brow! The word used here does not usually refer to the diadem of power, but to the crown won in conflict; and it is very remarkable that it should be said that, when Christ comes to judge the world, he will wear the garland of victory, the crown which he has won in the great battle which he has fought. How significant of his final triumph will that crown of gold be about those brows that were once covered with bloody sweat when he was fighting the battle for our salvation!"

John also records the angel's declaration:

"...for the harvest of the earth is ripe."

The Greek word translated "ripe" carries the idea of something that has become fully mature—even overripe or dried up—and is ready for immediate harvest. The picture is not of fruit prematurely gathered but of a harvest that has reached the point where delay is no longer appropriate.

This imagery reminds us that God's judgment is never rushed. Throughout history, the Lord has demonstrated extraordinary patience toward sinful humanity. Generation after generation has received His mercy, His warnings, and His invitation to repent. Even during the Tribulation itself, God sends the Two Witnesses, the 144,000, and angelic messengers proclaiming the everlasting Gospel to the entire world.

The harvest therefore comes only after every opportunity for repentance has been extended.

Peter reminds us:

"The Lord is not slack concerning His promise, as some count slackness, but is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance." (2 Peter 3:9)

God's delay in judgment should never be mistaken for indifference toward sin. Rather, it is evidence of His remarkable patience and mercy. Yet there comes a point when His longsuffering reaches its appointed conclusion, and justice must finally be executed.

Joseph Seiss writes:

"It must be remembered that evil has its harvest as well as good. There is a harvest of misery and woe—a harvest for the gathering, binding, and burning of the tares—as well as for the gathering of the wheat into the garner of Heaven."

This observation reflects a truth taught throughout Scripture. Every seed produces a harvest. Faithfulness bears the fruit of eternal life, while persistent rebellion ultimately yields judgment. Jesus Himself spoke of both harvests in His parable of the wheat and the tares (Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43), where the righteous are gathered into His kingdom while the wicked are separated for judgment.

By the time Revelation 14 unfolds, humanity has reached the full measure of its rebellion against God. The Antichrist has established his global kingdom. The False Prophet has deceived the nations. The world has embraced the worship of the beast while rejecting repeated calls to repentance. Sin has reached its full maturity.

The earth is now "ripe."

The time for sowing has ended. The time for reaping has arrived.

The One who once came as the suffering Servant now appears as the righteous Judge. The Savior who stretched out His hands upon the cross now stretches forth His sickle. The Lamb who offered Himself for the sins of the world now prepares to judge the world that has rejected Him.

The harvest has come, and the Judge of all the earth will do what is perfectly just.

text:
Script: Scene 1 — Opening instrumental

Before dawn inside their quiet palace chamber. Andromache stands beside an open window while Troy’s distant towers glow beneath a fading moon. A cold breeze lifts the linen curtains and moves strands of her hair. Behind her, Hector’s bronze armor rests beside their bed. She turns toward it with dread.

Scene 2 — “They call you the shield of the city”

Hector stands before a polished bronze mirror as Andromache carefully places his heavy red cloak over his shoulders. Morning light catches the edges of his armor. He appears powerful in the reflection, but Andromache watches him with quiet fear.

Scene 3 — “The strongest man beneath the sun”

Brief transition to Hector walking through Troy in warm sunlight. Citizens step aside and look toward him with admiration. Children pretend to fight with wooden swords, copying him. Hector offers them a gentle smile, but Andromache watches from behind a column, separated from the cheering crowd.

Scene 4 — “But I know your patience and pity”

Warm memory: Hector sits on the palace floor without armor, smiling while repairing a small wooden horse. Andromache sits beside him, leaning affectionately against his shoulder. Their domestic chamber glows with amber evening light.

Scene 5 — “And the way you hold our little one”

Hector lifts their laughing toddler into the air and catches him against his chest. Andromache watches them from the doorway, smiling softly. Hector kisses the child’s curls while the boy grabs his beard. This should feel like their happiest memory.

Scene 6 — “I fasten your cloak at the shoulder”

Return to the cold final morning. Close-up of Andromache’s trembling fingers fastening the round gold clasp at Hector’s shoulder. Her hand lingers against his chest. Hector gently covers her hand with his own.

Scene 7 — “You swear you’ll return with the light”

Hector raises Andromache’s hand and kisses her fingers. He gives her a small reassuring smile, then touches his forehead to hers. She closes her eyes, wanting to believe him, while pale dawn grows behind them.

Scene 8 — “But the morning is growing colder”

A gust enters through the chamber window and extinguishes an oil lamp. The palette drains from warm gold into cold blue-grey. Andromache opens her eyes as Hector slowly pulls away from her.

Scene 9 — “And your eyes have gone to the fight”

Close-up of Hector turning toward the open doorway. Beyond it, armed Trojan soldiers wait in the courtyard while distant war banners move in the wind. Andromache remains close to him, but his gaze is already fixed on the gates.

Scene 10 — “Let Troy lose her towers / Let Troy lose her throne”

Andromache rushes after Hector onto a high palace terrace. She grabs his hand as Troy stretches majestically behind them. In her fearful imagination, the towers darken and crumble into drifting ash, but she never takes her eyes off him.

Scene 11 — “What good is a kingdom if I’m left alone?”

The imagined city disappears into darkness. For one symbolic moment, Andromache stands completely alone in an empty throne room. Hector’s red cloak slips through her fingers and falls onto the marble floor.

Scene 12 — First chorus

Back in reality, Andromache holds both of Hector’s hands and desperately searches his face. As she sings, fleeting warm memories move around them like living paintings: their wedding beneath olive branches, walking together through palace gardens, and Hector wrapping his cloak around her in the rain.

Scene 13 — “Long before they called you Hector”

Hector removes his bronze helmet, becoming simply her husband again. Andromache touches his cheek while he leans into her palm. The cheering soldiers beyond the courtyard become silent and blurred, leaving only the two of them in focus.

Scene 14 — “Leave your sword beside the doorway”

Andromache takes Hector’s hand and guides it toward the sword at his waist, silently pleading with him to remove it. For a moment, his fingers begin to loosen the belt. Then a distant war horn sounds. He stops.

Scene 15 — “They may need you for their glory”

The great gates of Troy open. Hundreds of soldiers lift their spears as Hector approaches. Andromache stands at the top of the palace steps holding their child, painfully small against the enormous city and its army.

Scene 16 — “But I need you most of all”

Hector stops and turns back. Across the courtyard, he and Andromache look directly at each other. She mouths his name. He takes one step toward her—but the soldiers move forward, carrying him away with them like a tide.

Scene 17 — Bridge: “Our child cried beneath your helmet”

At the gate, their toddler becomes frightened by Hector’s tall horsehair plume and hides against Andromache. Hector immediately kneels, removes his helmet and places it on the ground. His expression softens completely.

Scene 18 — “You held him close and kissed him”

Hector takes the child into his arms, kisses his forehead and makes him laugh through his tears. He places one hand gently over the boy’s head in blessing. Andromache watches, trying not to cry as distant drums grow louder.

Scene 19 — Final chorus begins

Hector hands the child back to Andromache and puts on his helmet. He walks through the gates without looking back at first. Andromache follows for several steps, but the massive gates slowly close between them.

Scene 20 — “Though she led you to the flame”

From the city wall, Andromache watches the distant battlefield beneath a blood-red sunset. We see Hector only as a small red-cloaked figure moving toward an opposing warrior beneath swirling dust. Do not show the fight or Hector dying.

Scene 21 — “They will sing about your courage”

The soundless battlefield dissolves into a painted mural of Hector standing triumphantly with his spear. Trojan citizens gather beneath it with candles and flowers, already transforming the real man into an untouchable legend.

Scene 22 — “I will whisper out your name”

Andromache sits alone inside their dark chamber, wearing Hector’s red cloak around her shoulders. She holds his gold clasp in her palm and whispers his name. Tears finally fall, but her grief remains quiet and restrained.

Scene 23 — “They may call you Troy’s great hero”

Warm memories of Hector flicker across the chamber walls: Hector laughing, holding their child, sleeping beside Andromache and turning toward her with his familiar gentle smile. The heroic mural outside fades while these private memories remain bright.

Scene 24 — “But you were my home before the war”

In a dreamlike golden field, Andromache sees Hector without armor, dressed in his simple red tunic. He stands beneath an olive tree and reaches out his hand. She almost reaches him—but he begins dissolving into glowing golden dust.

Scene 25 — “Before Troy took it all”

Return to the palace chamber at sunrise. Andromache stands at the same window from the opening, holding their sleeping child against her chest. Hector’s empty armor remains behind her. She closes her fist around his gold clasp as sunlight slowly fills the room. The camera pulls out beyond the window, leaving her framed inside the vast city of Troy. Fade to black.

text:
When a single F35 stealth jet crashes, either during a combat mission or during a routine training exercise, media headlines immediately focus on the staggering financial loss. Millions of dollars vanished in a single instant. Yet inside defense planning rooms, money isn't what makes the loss agonizing.

A defense economist sat opposite a military fleet scheduler, looking at the crash report. The economist assumed the panic was about capital allocation.

"The unit cost sits around $80 million," the defense economist noted. "In an annual defense budget exceeding $850 billion, $80 million is less than 0.01%. We can write a check tomorrow to cover the replacement. Why is the Air Force treating this like an operational disaster?"

The fleet scheduler shook his head. "If you hand us $80 million today, when do you think we get the jet?"

"Next month?" the economist guessed. "Or by the end of the quarter?"

"Try three years," the fleet scheduler replied. "Money doesn't build stealth fighters. Specialized manufacturing lines with fixed throughput build them. Every factory slot for the next 36 months is already booked for existing unit deliveries and foreign military sales. You can't buy a replacement off a dealer lot."

The economist paused as the financial assumption collapsed. The primary constraint wasn't capital. It was time and fixed physical capacity.

"So the squadron is simply down one jet for three years," the economist reasoned. "That's inconvenient, but surely five operational jets can absorb the workload of six?"

"That's where the second breakdown happens," the scheduler explained. "Pilot qualification requires a strict minimum number of monthly flight hours. When you remove one airframe from a six jet flight line, those required hours don't vanish. You must distribute those flight hours across the remaining five airframes."

"Which accelerates their physical wear," the economist realized.

"Exactly," the scheduler said. "You force the remaining airframes to fly 20% more hours per month. That pushes them into heavy maintenance cycles much faster, which triggers component fatigue and pulls even more jets off the active flight line. Losing one airframe creates a compounding availability trap across the entire squadron."

The economist stared at the flight readiness charts. The missing jet wasn't just a lost asset. It was a structural load bearing pillar whose removal forced extra stress onto every surviving node in the system.

"What happens if the crash occurs over international waters?" the scheduler asked, pushing the problem further.

"You launch a search and rescue mission for the pilot," the economist offered.

"And then you must deploy an entire naval task force to guard or retrieve the wreckage on the ocean floor," the scheduler added.

"Why?"

"Because of the technology on board?"

"Because stealth isn't just a geometry," the scheduler said. "It's a delicate balance of radar absorbing materials, electronic warfare signal libraries, and sensor fusion algorithms. If an adversary recovers even a square meter of damaged skin panel or radar array from the seabed, they can measure its exact electromagnetic response. That single recovered piece allows them to recalibrate their ground radar systems, potentially neutralizing the low observability of all 1,000 F35 aircraft operating worldwide."

The economist saw the complete picture. The true cost of losing a single stealth jet has almost nothing to do with its price tag. Reality enforces three strict constraints: a manufacturing pipeline that takes years to deliver a single unit, a fleet ecosystem where losing one airframe degrades the lifespan of all others, and a security envelope where physical loss threatens the entire global fleet's combat edge.

Heather Cox Richardson Aug 1, 2026

Courtney Kube, Monica Alba, Peter Nicholas, Gordon Lubold, Katherine Doyle, and Andrea Mitchell of NBC News reported Wednesday that President Donald J. Trump is “exasperated” that the Iran war is dragging on and that his advisors can’t agree what to do next. Reportedly, he erupted last week during a meeting with his national security team, shouting expletives at the officials in the room. One of Trump’s allies told the reporters that Trump had not expected the war to last as long as it has. “There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint.... He did not intend this to be a long, drawn-out war,” the person said.

Yesterday the war began to widen as a drone hit a gas storage tanker owned by a U.S. company in Egypt near the Suez Canal—no one has claimed responsibility—and Iran struck at American installations in Jordan. U.S. and Saudi Arabian forces launched strikes against Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.

At a Cabinet meeting at Camp David today, Trump told reporters he intends to hit Iran with heavy military strikes again to force Iranian negotiators to give in to his demands. “We will be hitting them very hard,” he said. “And you know at some point, they’re going to say, ‘We just can’t take it anymore.’” “We just want to win,” he said. “We’re doing very well.”

Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not appear to have a strategy for their war on Iran. Instead, they had an ideology. That ideology elevates individualism over the idea behind the modern American state: that government should regulate business, maintain a basic social safety net, promote infrastructure, protect civil rights, and support an international order based in rules rather than in military might.

Since the 1950s, opponents of that modern state have celebrated the American individual, especially the American cowboy, as the figure the American government should privilege and protect. In their mythology, the cowboy wanted nothing from the government but to be left alone to rise through his own hard work, protecting himself and his family from wrongdoers with his gun and his principles. The education, expertise, cooperation, and coalitions on which the modern U.S. stood before Trump were signs not of strength, but of weakness.

That ideology seems to have been what was behind the attack on Iran. In 2015 the U.S., China, France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom, and Iran negotiated the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). Under the JCPOA, Iran agreed to reduce its stockpile of enriched uranium significantly and allow inspections, in exchange for relief from some sanctions. The Strait of Hormuz remained open. Although inspectors said Iran was honoring the deal, Trump maintained it was “[o]ne of the worst deals ever made by our Country.” He took the U.S. out of the JCPOA in 2018, and the following year, Iran resumed work on enriched uranium necessary for a nuclear weapon.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth brought this ideology into the Defense Department, which he tried to rebrand the “Department of War.” In 2024, Hegseth published a book titled The War on Warriors: Behind the Betrayal of the Men Who Keep Us Free. In it, he claimed that the U.S. military was weak and “effeminate” because its leaders had embraced diversity, equity, and inclusion.

His prescription for the country involved getting rid of the Geneva Conventions, which recognize human rights for noncombatants in war, claiming they forced the U.S. troops to fight “with one hand behind our back.” In his confirmation hearings, Hegseth refused to tell Senator Angus King (I-ME) that he would honor those agreements.

On September 5, 2025, Hegseth said changing the name of the Defense Department to the Department of War was part of his campaign to spread a “warrior ethos” at the Pentagon. The rebranding, he said, was part of “restoring intentionality to the use of force…. We’re going to go on offense, not just on defense. Maximum lethality, not tepid legality, violent effect, not politically correct. We’re going to raise up warriors, not just defenders. So this War Department, Mr. President, just like America, is back.”

But Trump’s war on Iran has illustrated the weakness of that vision. Trump reiterated yet again today that the U.S. has dominated Iran’s military. “They’re being decimated. They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no anti-aircraft,” he said. But for all that, they retain their ability to choke world trade by controlling the Strait of Hormuz—the very condition previous presidents worked to avoid through negotiations.

An article yesterday by Politico senior foreign affairs correspondent Nahal Toosi suggests that the “cowboy” approach to foreign policy has another downside. Toosi called out the extreme attacks of Trump and his aides on the International Criminal Court (ICC) and wrote that, although the U.S. is not a signatory to that court, former government officials and legal scholars suspect Trump and administration officials are worried about future prosecutions.

On July 13, Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in the Wall Street Journal that the administration intends to “dismantle the ICC—brick by brick, if necessary.” A press release from the State Department on the same day said that the U.S. “will feature a whole-of-government response to systematically disable the ICC’s ability to operate, target American servicemen or officials, or otherwise threaten American sovereignty.”

A Republican operative close to the White House, Bill Cortese, told Toosi that some administration officials are afraid that “if Democrats come into power…, an unchecked ICC and other international institutions are going to unleash a wave of litigation against this administration and anyone associated with it.” Toosi notes that during the administration, U.S. law enforcement and military officials have been accused of human rights violations that reach across borders.

Notably, on September 2, 2025, three days before Hegseth’s “maximum lethality, not tepid legality” speech, the administration began strikes against small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. Those strikes have killed more than 220 people, but the administration has offered no evidence to prove its claims that those killed were “narcoterrorists” killed to stop the flow of cocaine to the U.S.

Trump claims the strikes have virtually ended drug trafficking by sea, but on July 27, Alex Horton, Terrence McCoy, Samantha Schmidt, and Dylan Moriarty of the Washington Post reported that according to Pentagon officials and officials from the Drug Enforcement Agency, the strikes have not reduced the cocaine coming into the U.S. Indeed, the dropping price of the drug suggests there is more of it now than there was a year ago. Instead, the strikes have simply prompted criminal organizations to find new routes. The strikes have also disrupted the law enforcement system in which lower-level participants inform on higher-ups, as the lower-level sources are being pulled back.

While the strikes appear to have done little to stop the flow of drugs, legal analysts say they look a lot like former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte’s extrajudicial killings of suspected drug dealers and users. Law professor Charlie Trumbull reminded readers of Foreign Policy that in 2017, Trump called Duterte to congratulate him for doing “an unbelievable job on the drug problem.” Trumbull also noted that “Duterte is now behind bars in the Hague,” charged with crimes against humanity for trying to get rid of criminals by unlawful means, including murder.

“The Trump administration should be concerned,” Trumbull warned.

On July 25 the U.S. State Department cheered Venezuela’s withdrawal from the treaty that established the ICC and said it welcomed “the new Venezuelan government’s partnership on American-led efforts to dismantle the corrupt and worthless ICC.” It continued, “The ICC is neither credible, independent, nor legitimate,” and called on all members of the ICC to abandon it.

Today Missy Ryan and Nancy A. Youssef of The Atlantic reported that in the wake of the U.S. strike on the Minab school that killed 168 people, mostly schoolchildren, in the first hours of the war, the Pentagon is considering reversing some of the deep cuts Hegseth made to the staff at the Defense Department. A report by the Pentagon inspector general found that cuts to the civilian-harm protections staff who work to protect noncombatants may have violated laws.

Ryan and Youssef explain that the U.S. military had spent decades building its civilian protections. Leaders understood that battlefield victories were insufficient to win military operations and that protecting civilians is crucial to public support for those operations. Ryan and Youssef noted that to reflect this understanding, the Pentagon in 2006 “formally added legitimacy, restraint, and perseverance to its Principles of Joint Operations, defining legitimacy as ‘the legality, morality, and rightness of the actions undertaken.’”

A U.S. official told Ryan and Youssef that the leadership of U.S. combat commands uniformly support the restoration of the personnel whose job it is to protect civilians. But Hegseth has not committed to the restoration of the old system, the journalists note, and even if he does, it will have little effect unless he changes his own rhetoric.

For his part, Trump appears to be addressing concerns about future prosecutions, whether by the ICC or at U.S. courts, by keeping control of the government after the midterms. Today Trump disagreed with the assessment of investigators that a recent cyberattack on municipal water systems in Minnesota was likely the work of Iranian hackers. Instead, he blamed Democrats.

“We heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack and they blame it on Iran,” he told reporters. “I don’t think so. I think. I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent. There was a cyberattack of thirty water plants. And I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota.”

There is another piece of evidence this week that the abandonment of education and expertise in favor of a “warrior ethos” has weakened the U.S. on the world stage. At an international conference on AIDS in Rio de Janeiro, an official of the U.S. State Department showed a map of Africa on which six fake countries were identified with the names of random real countries—including Nigeria, where several hundred U.S. soldiers are deployed. Reuters identified the image as AI.

Attendees took screenshots and posted them online. “Whoever ⁠created and approved this slide did not know where countries in Africa are and did not care to check their work,” one wrote.

CHIEF KEFAS W. ROPSHIK: A LIFETIME OF GRATITUDE TO A FATHER, A LEADER, AND A LEGEND AT 80, BABA JONAH D. JANG

Some memories never fade. They become part of who we are.

In the late 1980s as a young boy in Makurdi, I witnessed an act of kindness that I could not fully understand at the time, but one that would remain etched in my heart forever. Then Military Administrator of Benue State, Baba Jonah David Jang, saw a need in my family and responded with quiet generosity. He offered my father a Peugeot 505 to enable him convey our family from Benue to Shendam. To many, it may have seemed like a simple gesture. To our family, it was life-changing. Decades have passed, yet that singular act of compassion has remained one of my earliest and most enduring memories of a man whose greatness has always been expressed not merely through the offices he occupied, but through the lives he touched.

Today, as I celebrate Baba at 80, I do so not only as a political associate, but as someone whose life has been personally enriched by his kindness, mentorship, and fatherly affection. The little boy who benefited from his generosity has grown into a man privileged to call him a political father. Life has a remarkable way of bringing its stories full circle.

Baba Jonah David Jang's life is the very definition of purposeful service. From the discipline of the Nigerian Air Force to his stewardship as Military Governor of Gongola and Benue States, from his transformative years as Governor of Plateau State to his distinguished service in the Senate, every chapter of his journey has been marked by courage, conviction, and an unwavering commitment to the people. His vision laid the foundations of the modern Plateau we know today, while his steadfast defence of justice, peace, and the dignity of our people has earned him a place among the most respected leaders our state has produced.

What has always distinguished Baba is not simply his record in public office, but his humanity. He has never measured leadership by power, but by service; never sought applause, but impact. Countless individuals and families, many of whose stories may never be publicly told, have experienced his generosity, compassion, and willingness to lift others without expecting anything in return. My family is proud to be among them.

As I reflect on the journey of this extraordinary man, I am reminded that true greatness is not defined by titles, but by the enduring influence one leaves on generations. Baba has inspired leaders, nurtured young people, defended the vulnerable, and remained steadfast in his love for Plateau State and Nigeria. His life is a lesson in integrity, resilience, sacrifice, and selfless leadership.

On this historic occasion of your 80th birthday, Baba, I offer my deepest gratitude for all you have been to me, my family, Plateau State, and our nation. Thank you for believing in people. Thank you for leading with courage. Thank you for showing that genuine leadership is rooted in compassion.

May Almighty God continue to preserve you in excellent health, renew your strength daily, and grant you many more years filled with peace, joy, and fulfilment. May your wisdom continue to guide generations, your legacy continue to inspire, and your life remain a shining testament to what selfless leadership truly means.

Happy 80th Birthday, Baba.

Your story is still inspiring. Your legacy is still growing. And your impact will continue to live on in the hearts of those you have touched—including mine.

Chief Kefas Wungak Ropshik
Gubernatorial Candidate
PDP Plateau

🇺🇸 U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command (SSC) has awarded two agreements to BAE Systems and Trimble Military and Advanced Systems to support development of a next-generation Maritime and Aviation Receiver Card (MAVRC) military GPS user equipment receiver. @USSpaceForce @USSF_SSC @BAESystemsInc 

The contract was awarded on behalf of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center's (AFLCMC) Electronic Systems Directorate. @AFLCMCofficial 

These agreements will support requirements development, risk reduction studies, and documentation for a design concept review milestone. The effort is the first phase in a two-part approach that will inform future prototyping, demonstrations, and integration and testing to produce a GPS M-code receiver for maritime and aviation platforms.

MAVRC is designed to provide weapons system integrators with more resilient positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) capabilities in contested environments. The system is expected to improve anti-jam and anti- spoof performance, SWaP demands, and include Regional Military Protection (RMP). It is also expected to offer backward compatibility with MGUE Increment 1 aviation and maritime receivers while minimizing integration cost.

A subset of the awardees will move forward to the next phase, which will include a Final Design Review and prototype development. The target prototype delivery is 2031.

Outcome of that tasking is still  Drawer 7. [The secret drawer where the REAL TRUTH is] Really puts BUILDING 7 & 7TH FLOOR into perspective doesn't it. This is getting less random as I type this out. SARs as opening fuel puts FinCEN/Treasury in the comparison class with  CFIUS/State/DOE. Different agencies, different paper. Grassley asked for  the SARs first for a reason.

Hidden hand, said carefully: the useful move for anyone who needed this not to become a 2018–2020 charging decision was not a press conference saying  “innocent.”

EXPANDING ON 18 US CODE 3287 ****PLEASE PAY CLOSE ATTENTION****

Ross was not citing a vibe. He was citing a specific statute because, without it, a lot of the 2010 CFIUS-era conduct would already have been  dead by June 2018.

What 18 U.S.C. § 3287 actually says

It is the Wartime Suspension of Limitations Act (WSLA). 

In plain English:

When the United States is at war, or Congress has passed a specific  authorization to use the Armed Forces (the kind described in the War Powers Resolution), the ordinary criminal clock stops running for three kinds of offenses:

Fraud or attempted fraud against the United States or any U.S. agency — including by conspiracy.

Offenses tied to U.S. government property (getting it, holding it, selling it).

Offenses tied to war / AUMF contracting — bids, payments, performance, closeout  of contracts that are connected to the war or to the authorized use of  the armed forces.

The clock stays stopped until five years after hostilities are declared  over — by a presidential proclamation with notice to Congress, or by a  concurrent resolution of Congress.

That last sentence is the whole trick. The 2001 AUMF is still on the books.  There has never been a clean WSLA-style “hostilities are terminated”  proclamation that everyone treats as ending the 9/11 war for this  statute. So if a prosecutor can get a case into § 3287, a 2010 act can  still be alive in 2018 — and, on the same theory, in 2026.

Congress widened the statute in 2008 after courts had read “at war” tightly. The  amendment expressly says an AUMF counts as “war” for this section. That  is why a field prosecutor in Little Rock could even type the citation.

Default  federal clock, for contrast: most fraud / false-statement counts are  five years from the offense (§ 3282). CFIUS vote on Uranium One / ARMZ  is 2010-era. By June 1, 2018 you are past five years unless something  suspends or restarts the clock. That is the sentence in Ross’s email:  the U/O slice is “actually NOT time barred.”

What Ross was trying to do with it

From  the Grassley exhibit: most of Little Rock’s 17 FD-302s “pertain  directly to the Uranium One component… which as we have previously  discussed, is actually NOT time barred by a statute of limitations” —  and the exhibit text points at § 3287. In the same email he says the  intel summary is weak on possible false statements to CFIUS to induce  authorization to sell U/O to Rosatom.

So the legal story he was keeping alive is not “Clinton sold the uranium, therefore treason.” 

It is closer to:

Someone may have lied to a U.S. agency (CFIUS, and/or DOE on the later export/trucking piece).

Lying to the United States to get a national-security sign-off is fraud against the United States (bucket 1).

Because an AUMF is in force and hostilities have not been terminated the WSLA way, the five-year clock never started to run out.

He also lists interviews still needed (Giustra, Telfer, Campbell, named  foreign nationals, the State career official Fernandez talked to, DOE  people on the Rosatom trucking firm). That is the work you do if you  believe the clock is still open.

Elsewhere  in the same traffic there is a more ordinary limitations idea: some theories die when a person leaves office. That is a different clock  (when the official act ended). § 3287 is the “war froze the fraud clock”  theory. 

Do not mash them together.

How well that theory actually fits Uranium One

What helps Ross

Bucket 1 is written broadly: fraud against “the United States or any agency  thereof in any manner.” CFIUS sits in Treasury’s building. A false  statement to CFIUS is, on a friendly reading, fraud on an agency of the  United States.

The 2008 text lets him use the 2001 AUMF as the “we are at war” on-switch without a declared war.

No termination proclamation means the suspension, if it applies, is still on in 2018 and still on in 2026.

False-statement  / concealment theories are exactly the kind of count you reach for when  the underlying “sold the committee” bribery story is old or thin.

What hurts Ross

Courts  fight over whether the phrase “connected with or related to the  prosecution of the war or … authorized use of the Armed Forces” limits  only the contracting bucket or all three buckets. If it limits all  three, a CFIUS mining deal in 2010 has to be tied to the AUMF war, not  just “fraud during years when an AUMF existed.” That is a hard sell.  Uranium in the ground in Wyoming is not a Humvee contract.

WSLA is a suspension statute. Judges construe those narrowly. You do not get extra years because the case is famous.

“Fraud  against the United States” is not the same as “donation to a foundation  while CFIUS voted.” Pay-to-play through a charity is a different  statute set (bribery, honest services after McDonnell, FARA, etc.), many  of which are not automatically WSLA offenses. 

We're more prepared now than ever to accept this difficult truth.

The  Jan 2018 slide said “no evidence found to date revealing influence  towards the U.O. acquisition.” § 3287 cannot create evidence. It can  only keep a door from locking if evidence later appears.

Even if the clock is open, someone still has to prove a false statement to  CFIUS (or another agency) by a chargeable person, beyond a donation  timeline. Ross himself said that work was unfinished.

Pile  A: a FAUSA in the district that held the 302s wrote, in 2018, that he  believed the U/O component was not dead on time, and he cited the  wartime statute.

Pile B: a court has held that this PI is WSLA-covered. It has not.

How it sits on the rest of the board

This  is why Grassley put Ross’s email next to the “no evidence to date”  slide. One document tells the public the acquisition-influence theory is  empty. The other tells a U.S. Attorney the clock on a  false-statement-to-CFIUS theory is still running and interviews remain.  Those can both be in the file. They are not the same claim.

It  also explains the 2020 punch list. If you think § 3287 applies, you do not close because 2010 was eight years ago. You keep asking for Giustra,  Telfer, Campbell, DOE export people, Weiner/Foundation server warrants.  If you think § 3287 does not apply, that list is theater and the case  should have been declined in writing. Grassley’s question 3 — what was  the outcome? — is the question that distinguishes those two worlds.

Same-rule  test: if a different administration used § 3287 to keep a 2010  CFIUS-fraud theory alive against the other tribe, you would still demand  the predicate (an actual false statement to the committee), not the  wartime caption alone. The AUMF we talked about as post-9/11 design is the same AUMF this statute rides on. That is not poetry. It is why a 2001 force resolution is still doing work in a 2018 Arkansas email about  a mining company.

What it does not mean

It does not make Uranium One a war crime.

It does not toll every Clinton Foundation allegation. Band/State  meeting-coordination, Haiti permits, Boeing pledges — each count has its  own clock and its own statute.

It does not bind Blanche or Patel. They can adopt Ross’s theory, reject it, or produce the 302s and let a USA decide.

It does not open the Supreme Court. SCOTUS would only see this if someone  charged a stale count and a defendant moved to dismiss as time-barred.  Then a justice would have to decide how far bucket 1 stretches during an  un-terminated AUMF. That case does not exist yet.

Bottom line for the desk.

§ 3287 is the legal reason Little Rock could say in 2018 “not time barred.”

It is a clock tool for fraud on the United States while an AUMF is live.  It is not a substitute 302. If the missing interviews and SARs never show a lie to CFIUS, the wartime statute is a key to an empty room. If they do, the key is why that room was never allowed to be called closed. @CFWBers 

This is The American Desk. 

This is how we will judge moving forward. 

Together. 

We, The People.

Confessions of an AI Editor
At the start-up I worked for, I was judged not by my ability to be a good reader but by my capacity to become one with a machine.
Diya Isha
Outdoor typewriting class for secretaries, 1932.(Imagno / Getty Images)

It was ironic that the literary services start-up had been founded by an editor. But if you’d met her, that wouldn’t surprise you. The labor of editing, she believed, was arduous and its romanticization undeserved. To her, the taste of selection was the sole editorial virtue, everything else a chore. In her ideal world, each piece of copy would already come with tracked changes, leaving the prudent editor with little more than the discretion to press “Accept” or “Reject.” She would happily relegate the rest of the labor and presumed others would feel this way too. And so, when she created her company, she gave away all the “drudgery” to the thing, an artificial-intelligence tool. Like Pygmalion, she built it in her image, and like Pygmalion, she loved what she had wrought. Even if she might hesitate to call it flawless, it was preferable to the many entry-level copy editors who routinely sent in their CVs, eager to do her bidding. After all, the thing could produce an editorial memo in less than a minute. In a few seconds, it could parse a tangled paragraph and downsize it to a corporatized readability, or copy-edit a chapter in the time it takes to shift between browsers. “I taught it as I taught you,” my boss said. With her tool by my side, I could edit a piece of prose without so much as reading a line.

My boss would sit at her long, lonely desk for hours, the picture of a classic editor. Her rainbow-coded bookcase was the work of a handsomely paid book stylist who, I imagined, read only the spines. When I interrupted her, she would tap her glasses till they landed, precisely each time, on the edge of her nose, a compliment to the gravity of her downward glare. This editorial chic perhaps served to make the uncool, fraught endeavour of using artificial intelligence for the time-honored work of editing appear less offensive. At parties, I could never admit where I worked. It was like lying about a bad boyfriend.

The type of tool my boss’s company had created was christened, sometimes pejoratively, an “AI wrapper.” For a tool created by “wrapping” foundation models with an interface inviting enough to goad you into buying yet another subscription, “wrapper” is a fitting descriptor. All a company has to do to make one is pretty up the existing Big AI models. On the back end, the system instructions my boss had written would begin, “You are a diligent editor…,” and once you uploaded a manuscript onto the thing, it would answer with the disarming confidence of one. The first time I used it to line-edit a chapter of a book, the sight of the text being pressed into cohesion was spectacular.

In the initial days of the job, I’d judge the thing’s judgment and report back on any of its transgressions. As I occupied the lowest rung of the editorial ladder, I couldn’t even say that I was training it to replace me. When it was right, it was right, and when it was wrong, we were wrong: All the blame for its hallucinations was to be shared with the human who bungled the prompt my boss offered it.
Reader-Funded since 1865
This article has been made free to read. Keeping it that way isn't.
Donate

My condition at the company became only more demoralizing when I tried to humanize the thing as a means of selling it to clients. (If I wanted to be a better editor, I also had to learn how to be a marketer, my boss reasoned.) Once, I called it my boss’s doppelgänger; other times, I pitched it as a patient, forgiving editor, one certain not to take forever to validate the writer. “Unless you run out of tokens,” I’d joke. “And, of course, you can bug it on the weekends,” my boss would say.

Although I was as compliant as workers come, I almost never read anything that one of our clients, a think tank, sent our way. I wasn’t equipped for the task; I’d never learned how to edit a policy paper. That was acceptable as long as I could pretend otherwise, a demonstration that came as easily as copying and pasting swaths of generated edits into a document.
Current Issue
Cover of September 2026 Issue
September 2026 Issue

A recent study in the journal Technology, Mind, and Behavior found that those who relied heavily on large-language-model tools felt no sense of ownership over the output they created with them. This could explain why any compliment to my editing occasioned a headache, as if I had yanked out a fistful of hair. Although I was great at my work, I was no good at it. I couldn’t have done it without the thing.

 The fact that the thing possesses a style does not mean it’s a good style. After taking stock of human writing, it assesses recurring sentence structures and grammatical tools. Then it mistakes all the recurrences, such as the recurrence of em dashes, for a necessary characteristic of good writing. Whatever we now chastise as literary affronts for their likeness to AI-generated writing were, before AI, a kind of writing that could be considered forgettable, or writing that aspired to be, but was not quite yet, good. As Laura Kipnis has written in Wired, large language models, through which the thing routed its edits, favor “pseudo-profundities” like delve and dive. The side effect of fraternizing with AI as much as I was expected to do was that I started to see the hand of the machine lurking in things it could never, ever have touched. In his literary manifesto A World of Sex, for example, Henry Miller uses the word delve twice, smartly. But when I saw it in his prose, I was jump-scared.

At work, I was instructed to do away with all the telling platitudinal verbs, slipping an innocent choice in their place, sometimes even replacing the em dashes with commas. Even when endorsing the thing and being up-front about using AI, it couldn’t seem like you’d used AI.

I started to become disillusioned just as the thing started gaining popularity. We two sole employees and an intern were assigned to line-edit an entire 150,000-word PhD dissertation in no more than three days. As with many of our edits by then, it was to be completed piecemeal, as if the pages of the manuscript were sliding across a conveyor belt, each of us assigned to specific tasks.

When I told my boss the goal was impossible, she noted that this was probably because we expected to take as much time on it as a “manual editor” would. (It would appear that we were the “assisted” editors.) There was not even enough time to push back on the request: With the thing, we were compelled to work faster, even if it was making many dubious edits, as the mention of the thing slowing us down would always be regarded as a defensive reflex on our part.

I could not manage, let alone fathom, such proficiency, and so I didn’t read more than a paragraph of that dissertation while editing it. I yielded to the thing absolutely in order to deliver results as the efficient machine I was expected to be. Soon enough, anticlimactically, the writer’s message announcing their love of the edits was forwarded to me, with an addendum from my boss: “I said it was all you!” This clarification was a fiction: Those edits were never going to be mine.

In his 1948 lecture “Good Readers and Good Writers,” Vladimir Nabokov states that a reader who begins a book with a “ready-made generalization” in mind is reading it from the “wrong end…. Nothing is more boring or more unfair to the author.” Yet the prompt library of the thing was lined with phrases that worked with such generalizations. Each draft, it was assumed, warranted a homogeneous approach; the only demarcation was its form. (We even had a prompt to edit poetry.) As I worked, my ambivalence toward everything I edited swelled. I’d habitually run anything I was assigned to do through the models. (I was often asked to gut-check “with” them.) If I wasn’t swift enough, I was reminded that I should’ve been, for any holdup was objectionable when these tools exist. Any time I edited withthe thing, which was most of the time, the metastasizing impact lingered long after the injury of using it ended.

A good reader, “a rereader,” Nabokov writes, can take in the “artistic delight” of the writer. The thing, with its numb productivity, had neither the time nor the ability for this vaunted part of the exercise. Using it, I learned that anyone could engineer prompts. Even someone like me, with all my inexperience of the world, could hastily type something like “proptedit shrt story” into a chatbot interface and watch it reliably spew out a coherent prompt for editing a short story. I knew I wasn’t really editing, but at times I had to believe I was. At work, I often couldn’t allow myself to confront the thought that several prompts of roughly a few hundred words detailing how to approach any type of manuscript would never match years of editorial experience. That would’ve compromised the enterprise entirely.

We can, in theory, train the thing to sound like us. I wager, perhaps vainly, that it will never sound as much like us as we will come to sound like it. Because how an idea is articulated matters as much as the idea itself. Would writers want an editor who will gulp their sentences down and spit them back as prose of an equivocating indistinguishability?

In his foreword to Editor to Author: The Letters of Maxwell E. Perkins, John Hall Wheelock quotes the French critic Hippolyte Taine, who wrote that a “great editor” is “an artist whose medium is the work of other men.” The thing was designed to make the art of editing less taxing. An editor, in my boss’s theory, could use AI and still edit with rigor, still take the same amount of time as she otherwise would reading and rereading. It was the time to exercise “taste” that my boss wanted to give back to editors, and in the case of clients who used the tool, she did just that. Whether they used that extra time to further mold a promising writer or simply accelerate the production line, though, I don’t know.

What I do know is that the thing produced the addictive feeling of providing editorial attention without the fact of ever having to put in the hours required to actually do so. In the infrequent event of a client complaining about flat, uninspiring edits, we would never go back and do the work ourselves, but simply adjust the back-end prompt or switch the model assigned to it. Other times, we’d accuse the clients of vanity or oversensitivity. Usually, though, they left moderately pleased with the revised output.

When I left the job two years ago, it was out of a selfish desire to stockpile the little conviction I still had in the value of my creative labor and my most necessarily complex abilities. I couldn’t even confess how morally repulsive I thought my role to be. And my leaving, of course, didn’t make a dent in the project of automation. With the thing, anyone on the precipice of acquiring skill will atrophy into an unskilled laborer before they’ve even had the chance to slip up.

When a technology is pitched, even if unpersuasively, as a democratizing entity, any counter-argument to its use is often dismissed as snobbish. But when the employment of this technology is detected in writing, it is often rightfully met with aversion. If those who are disadvantaged, be it by class or competence, were to rely on it unquestionably, it would only re-create, if not entrench, the preexistent pecking order.

When I’m writing, I don’t want to suspect that I sound like AI, and when I’m reading, I don’t want to suspect the writer of using it. This suspicion, I worry, turns the mind into mush, much the way the thing was likely to do. Although I’m now a fairly competent copy editor, I take hours longer than I’d like to. On the other hand, the thing made me, inadvertently, a better reader, by striving against its very being.

AI, in short, insults the writerly tradition. We need not, and should not, capitulate to the basest instincts of this lowly thing, and neither should we have to correct ourselves in anticipation of it. It is a dehumanizing way not only to read, but to be read. Worse still are those industries that believe the reader will read what isn’t written by a human. Perhaps she will, but perhaps she’s also not the reader one wishes to have. The good reader of a great writer, as Nabokov observes, tries “to grasp the individual magic of [the writer’s] genius and to study the style, the imagery, the pattern of his novels or poems.” Why would you resort to this delectably masochistic labor if the writer, or their editor, didn’t labor themselves?

text:
2026 XXII. Conundrum
Overall market backdrop / 整体市场大背景Over the past two weeks, global markets have been roiled by intertwined risks. Confrontation between the US and Iran in the Middle East intensified, alongside rising risks of Russia‑Ukraine conflict escalation. Geopolitics drove sharp swings in crude‑oil prices. / 过去两周全球市场受多重风险交织扰动。中东美伊对抗加剧，俄乌冲突升级风险抬头，地缘扰动油价宽幅震荡。
US July PCE inflation met expectations, yet long‑end US Treasury yields remained elevated. The US Treasury conducted informal Yield Curve Control (YCC), which failed to reverse rate trends but triggered short‑term speculative rallies in gold and BTC. / 美国 7 月 PCE 通胀符合预期，但美债长端收益率居高不下，财政部非正式实施收益率曲线控制（YCC），未能扭转利率走势，却催生黄金、BTC 短期投机脉冲行情。
At Jackson Hole, Warsh delivered hawkish remarks, prompting markets to price in possible Fed rate hikes in 2026. Slowing ARR growth at OpenAI and Anthropic fueled worries over weak end‑user AI demand and pressured AI hardware and cloud‑service valuations. / 杰克逊霍尔年会 Warsh 发表偏鹰言论，市场开始交易 2026 年内美联储加息；OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 收入增速不及预期，市场担忧 AI 终端需求证伪，AI 硬件、云厂商板块估值承压。
Global equities diverged: US equities traded choppily, pan‑AI tech stocks weakened; Japanese and Korean markets corrected alongside AI hardware; A‑shares saw structural repair within a stock‑flow‑only environment. / 全球股市分化，美股震荡、泛 AI 科技股走弱，日韩股市随 AI 硬件回调，A 股呈现存量博弈下的结构性修复。

Two unresolved core market contradictions lifting volatility / 市场两大核心未解矛盾，推升波动率Contradiction 1: Whether higher oil prices from Middle‑East tensions will re‑ignite US inflation and force Fed rate hikes. / 矛盾一：中东推高油价是否会再度抬升美国通胀，倒逼美联储加息。
Contradiction 2: Whether slowing large‑model ARR reflects peaking downstream AI demand, or tight computing‑supply inflating costs and suppressing latent B‑sector demand. / 矛盾二：大模型 ARR 收入放缓，究竟代表下游 AI 需求见顶，还是算力供给紧缺抬高成本，压制 B 端潜在需求。
With no definitive resolution for either contradiction, investors should avoid one‑sided bets. Build well‑diversified portfolios and prepare hedging scenarios for geopolitical, monetary‑policy and AI‑sector risks. / 两大矛盾暂无确定答案，建议投资者避免单边押注单一情景，构建分散均衡组合，针对地缘、货币政策、AI 产业三类风险做好对冲预案。

Geopolitical assessments / 地缘局势判断Middle East: Both the US and Iran face domestic vulnerabilities. High oil prices hurt US living costs and threaten November mid‑term‑election outcomes; Iran suffers domestic social stress from sanctions. Neither side is ready for meaningful compromise. Full‑scale war or binding long‑term peace is unlikely in the near term; friction will persist, creating tail risks for crude oil and equities. / 中东：美伊双方各有内部软肋。美国的痛点是高油价抬升民生成本，冲击 11 月中期选举；伊朗受制于制裁带来国内民生压力。但双方均不愿做出实质让步，短期不会爆发全面战争，也难达成长期和平协议，冲突维持摩擦反复，持续给原油、权益市场埋下尾部风险。
Russia‑Ukraine: Russia leverages higher oil prices to signal pressure on NATO; this is mostly strategic deterrence. Large‑scale near‑term escalation has low probability, but risk premia for risk assets and commodities will stay elevated. / 俄乌：俄罗斯借高油价窗口期向北约施压，释放冲突升级信号，更多属于战略威慑。短期大规模升级概率有限，但风险持续存在，抬升全球避险溢价，放大大宗商品波动。

Crude‑oil supply and trading framework / 原油供给与交易思路Physical oil supply has proven resilient. Strait‑related exports have recovered to 50 % of pre‑conflict levels; pipeline rerouting enables 60‑70 % of pre‑conflict Middle‑East oil exports. Barring black‑swan destruction of tankers or production facilities, WTI will likely range $80‑90/bbl, with limited near‑term upside above $100/bbl./ 原油实际供给韧性强，海峡原油出口已恢复至战前 50%，叠加管道分流，中东 60‑70% 原油可正常输出；若无产油设施遭袭等黑天鹅，WTI 原油大概率在 80‑90 美元 / 桶震荡，油价冲上 100 美元基础不足。
Trading tactics: Establish short positions in tranches if WTI rebounds to $90‑100/bbl; long positions offer better risk‑reward below $80/bbl. Prepare stop‑losses for black‑swan shocks. / 交易上，WTI 反弹至 90‑100 美元区间分批做空；回落至 80 美元下方做多盈亏比更高，需要警惕黑天鹅带来止损风险。

US fiscal intervention and dollar liquidity / 美国财政干预与流动性Treasury YCC had limited effect and could not resolve excess Treasury‑supply issues. Markets misread the intervention as de‑facto easing, spurring speculative gold and BTC rallies vulnerable to sharp reversals once YCC expectations fade. / 财政部 YCC 干预长债效果有限，无法解决美债供给过剩问题；但市场解读为变相宽松，推动黄金、BTC 投机上涨，干预预期证伪后价格存在快速回调风险。
Hawkish Jackson‑Hole rhetoric does not guarantee a September rate hike. Hawkish communication serves to manage inflation expectations. September policy hinges entirely on August CPI and PPI prints. The baseline view is for the Fed to hold rates steady: energy‑driven inflation pressure is moderate while shelter disinflation continues. / Jackson Hole 偏鹰讲话不等于 9 月一定加息。鹰派发言主要用于管理通胀预期。9 月加息与否完全取决于 8 月 CPI、PPI 数据。基准情景下，受能源拉动有限、房租下行，预计美联储 9 月维持利率不变。
The TGA‑driven liquidity bump is seasonal fiscal spending, not Fed easing. Longer‑term Treasury issuance plus QT drains system liquidity; the ON RRP buffer is nearly depleted. Markets remain in a liquidity‑constrained stock‑flow‑only regime with no systemic new money inflows. / TGA 账户回落带来的流动性属于季度财政季节性脉冲，并非美联储放水。中长期财政部持续发债叠加 QT 缩表，ON RRP 逆回购缓冲近乎耗尽；市场整体是存量博弈，没有系统性增量资金。

AI‑sector analysis: not a straightforward bubble / AI 产业辨析：不完全等同于泡沫Some investors warn of an AI bubble: huge compute infrastructure contrasts with far smaller disclosed large‑model ARR. The report acknowledges partial merit in this concern yet points out logical flaws. / 市场担忧 AI 泡沫：算力基建体量巨大，但大模型公开 ARR 收入规模远不足以覆盖算力资产回报。报告认为该观点有参考性，但存在逻辑偏差。
AI revenue streams extend beyond coding. Biotech simulation, industrial quality‑control, government‑private deployments and financial risk‑control generate significant demand. Many enterprises run open‑source models on‑premise; this compute spending is excluded from public ARR figures of closed‑API vendors. / AI 收入不只有编程（coding）赛道：生物医药、工业仿真、政务私有化部署、金融风控等政企采购需求旺盛；大量机构采用开源模型本地部署，这部分算力需求不计入公有云厂商 ARR 数据，被市场忽视。
Slowing ARR partly reflects supply‑side bottlenecks. Capital expenditure takes 1‑2 years to turn into usable compute. Scarce compute inflates service costs and holds back B‑sector adoption. As compute capacity expands and unit prices fall, suppressed latent demand should materialize. This follows Jevons’ Paradox: cheaper compute will expand total compute demand. Even if fundamentals remain sound, bearish market sentiment can still trigger share‑price drawdowns; diversification is required. / ARR 增速放缓部分来自供给瓶颈：算力硬件、机房配套存在 1‑2 年建设周期，资本开支不能立刻转化为可用算力。当前算力紧缺抬高使用成本，压制 B 端企业落地意愿；未来算力供给释放、价格下行后，被压制需求有望释放，算力符合杰文斯悖论，成本下降会进一步扩大全社会总算力需求。即便基本面需求没有证伪，市场悲观情绪依旧会造成股价冲击，需要分散避险。

Asset‑allocation views across major markets / 各大类资产配置观点US Treasuries: Initiate staggered long positions on 10‑year Treasury yields above 4.65 %. Do not chase short‑term YCC‑driven bond rallies; use stop‑loss disciplines. / 美债：10 年期美债收益率高于 4.65% 时分批做多；不追 YCC 带来的短期脉冲行情，冲高后布局，设置止损。
US equities: Pressured by tightening‑liquidity fears and AI‑demand doubts. Diversify; avoid over‑concentration in storage /optical modules. Favor cloud‑service providers, equipment and advanced foundries with solid cash flow; add high‑dividend defensives. Trim heavy AI‑hardware positions on rebounds. / 美股：受流动性收紧、AI 需求担忧双重压制，多空分歧大。建议分散配置，避免重仓存储、光模块；优选现金流稳健云厂商、设备、代工龙头，搭配高股息公用事业与防御板块；满仓 AI 硬件的投资者逢反弹降仓。
A‑shares: Risks largely digested in July‑August; September opens a repair window, with small‑caps leading large‑caps. Add on dips, prefer broad‑market ETFs. Balance compute‑semiconductor domestic substitution with high‑dividend banks /coal. Avoid pure‑theme stocks without earnings; raise overall exposure as offshore risk sentiment improves. / A 股：7‑8 月风险充分释放，9 月进入修复窗口，小票优先启动。建议逢跌加仓，优先宽基 ETF；均衡布局算力半导体国产替代 + 银行、煤炭等高股息，规避纯题材小票，等待海外风险偏好抬升仓位。
Hong‑Kong equities: Outflows from long‑term foreign investors persist. Recent rebounds stem mostly from short‑covering rather than trend reversal. Trade in bands with high‑dividend utilities and consumption names as core holdings; do not expand positions without major catalysts. / 港股：外资流出压力未解除，反弹多为空头回补，非趋势反转；以高股息公用事业、消费龙头做底仓做波段，无重磅催化不扩大仓位。
Japanese & Korean equities: Highly correlated to AI‑hardware cycles. Japan offers better diversification than Korea. Neither market merits heavy exposure; buy on pull‑backs. Monitor Samsung / SK Hynix buy‑back plans as key catalysts. / 日韩股市：高度绑定 AI 硬件。日本股市成分更多元，配置优先级高于韩国；均不宜重仓，回调分批低吸，关注三星、海力士回购方案。

Yen‑short trades are only suitable for short‑term band‑trading; do not hold shorts long‑term. / 外汇：做空日元主要依靠美日利差走阔，但面临地缘缓和、美国通胀降温、政府汇率干预三大风险，仅适合波段，禁止长期持有空单。

text:
Rescuing A Friend

Part 2

Infiltrating The Chimera

Our shuttle enters the main deck of Chimaera’s aft hanger bays in formation. I move us to hover over our designated location, ease back on the repulserlifts, there is a quiet clank of metal against metal, and the cargo shuttle touches gently down on the main deck. “Shuttle 37 down,” Skywalker says into the comm. “Awaiting further orders.” “Shuttle 37, acknowledged,” replies the controller over the comm. “Shut down all systems and prepare for unloading.”

“Got it,” Skywalker reaches his left hand to shut off the comm, but I reach out my right hand to hover above his, and Skywalker pauses so I can speak. “Control, this is my first cargo run. About how long until we’ll be able to leave?”, I ask with my voice carrying the right tone of idle curiosity. I relying on my own skills and judgement without preplanning this with Skywalker. “I suggest you make yourselves comfortable,” Control said dryly.

“We unload all the shuttles before any of you leave. Figure a couple of hours, at the least.” “Oh,” I reply shifting my voice to sounding taken aback. “Well. . . thanks. Maybe I’ll take a nap.” I sign off. “Good,” I tell Skywalker as I unstrap from the pilot’s seat and stand up. “That ought to give us enough time to get to the detention center and back.” “Let’s just hope that they haven’t transferred Karrde off the ship,” Skywalker replies.

He follows me to the back of the command deck and down the spiral stairway leading to the cargo hold below. “They haven’t,” I reply. Skywalker stays with me and catches up on the stairway. “The only danger is that they might have started the full treatment already,” I continue.  Skywalker frowns down at me, “The full treatment?” “Their interrogation,” I walk out from the stairs, reach the middle of the hold, and look around at the floor.

“All right. Just about. . . there should do it,” I decide and gesture to a section of the deck in front of us. “Out of the way of prying eyes and you shouldn’t hit anything vital.” “Right,” Skywalker agrees with my choice of location. He walks over to the place I indicated, ignites his vibrant emerald lightsaber, and begins carefully cutting through the base of the shuttle. Skywalker moves judiciously and starts creating a circular hole that will be big enough for us to pass through.

Halfway along the sweep there is a spark, the lights go out around us, and Skywalker stops cutting. “It’s okay,” he reassures me as I curse quietly. “My lightsaber gives off enough light to see by.” The vibrant emerald glow of his lightsaber is incredibly bright in the dark room, illuminating the hold, Skywalker’s face, arms, and black Jedi robes. “I’m more worried that the cable might have arced to the hangar deck,” I explain.

“They couldn’t help but notice that.” Skywalker pauses, his eyes focus, and he reaches out with the Force to get a sense of the Chimera’s deck crew. “Nobody nearby seems to have seen anything,” Skywalker tells me. “We’ll hope,” I reply and gesture at the half-finished hole. “Get on with it.” It is curious that I could use my Force sense to find Skywalker in deep space when our ship was passing in hyperspace but I cannot sense the status of the nearby deck crew.

Skywalker’s vivid blue eyes lock with my emerald green eyes. He is staying alert to my emotional state, can sense that there is more to my annoyance then wanting Skywalker to slicing through the hull faster. I should be able to sense the people around me when we are not near ysalamiri. Skywalker does not comment, resumes the circular sweep of his emerald lightsaber through the shuttle’s hull, and finishes the cut a minute later.

We use a magnetic winch to lift up the piece of decking and outer haul into the hold. I move to stand across from Skywalker and we look at the hanger bay deck a few centimeters farther down, lit by the emerald glow of Luke’s lightsaber. I crouch, attach the cargo hold wench’s grapple to the visible section of the hanger bay deck, stand up again, and wait by the controls. Skywalker lowers himself to his knees then he stretches out on his abs across the cargo hold deck.

He extends his emerald lightsaber through the hole, pauses with his head tilted slightly to his right, and waits attentively. Skywalker is likely waiting for the deck below us to clear of personal. I think of something important. “Don’t forget to bevel it,” I remind Skywalker as his lightsaber begins to slide smoothly into the hard metal. “A gaping hole in the ceiling will be a little to oblivious for even conscripts to miss.”

Skywalker listens to me, nods in agreement, and completes the beveled cut. The wench grapple is still holding the piece of the deck and I am ready to activate it. Skywalker rises back to his knees and shins, and powers down his lightsaber. I activate the wrench and it hoists the piece upward. Skywalker watches the wench pull the slab up into the shuttle. I let it rise to a meter above the hold deck then stop the wench.

“That’s far enough,” I announce about the wench, draw my blaster, and hold it ready in my right hand. I lower myself to a crouch, sit gingerly on the edge of the warm hole, slide forward, and drop lightly through the hole. I use the Force to slow my descent, bend my knees, and land gracefully on the deck below. I straighten, look both ways down the corridor, and call quietly up to Skywalker, “All clear.”

Skywalker moves to sits on the edge of the hole, looks at the winch control, uses Force push to press the switch, and leaps through the hole. On the way down Skywalker realizes the drop is farther than he thought, bends his knees, and uses his Force enhanced muscles to absorb the impact that would normal cause injury. Skywalker lands gracefully beside me and recovers his balance. We look up at the gray metallic ceiling and see the plug has lowered back into its hole.

“Looks pretty good,” I say softly. “I don’t think that anyone will notice.” “Not unless they look up,” Skywalker agrees then looks around us. “Which way to the detention center?” “There,” I reply and gesture to our left and up with my blaster. “We’re not going there dressed like this, though. Come now.” I lead the way up the passage, along a crossway, and we start up a wider corridor. Skywalker is staying alert but there is currently no one near us.

“Awfully quiet down here,” Skywalker comments. “It won’t last,” I assure him. “This is a service supply area, and most of the people who’d normally be working here are a level up helping unload the shuttles. But we need to get into some uniforms of flight suits or something before we go much farther.” I guide us along another passage, through a crossway, and to another wide corridor.

Skywalker considers this. “Okay, but let’s try to avoid stormtrooper armor,” he says. “Those helmets are hard to see through.” My eyes narrow at that statement. Skywalker has worn stormtrooper armor before. “I didn’t think that Jedi needed to use their eyes,” I reply bitterly, the vision of my master’s death and the need to avenge him are an ache. The voice in my mind tells me, “You will kill, Luke Skywalker. You Will Kill, Luke Skywalker! I push it away with effort.

We keeping moving through the ship. “Watch it—here we are. That’s a section of crew quarters over there.” Skywalker shifts beside me as he feels the change in human population level and considers how best to handle the larger amount of people we are going to encounter. “I don’t think we can sneak through that many people,” Skywalker warns. “I wasn’t planning to,” I respond and gesture to another corridor leading off to our right.

“There should be a group of TIE pilot ready rooms down that way. Let’s see if we can find an empty one that has a couple of spare flight suits lying around.” Skywalker and I continue on. It is laxed that the Empire is leaving its service supply areas and corridors unguarded but helpful for us at the moment. Skywalker and I make our way down this corridor. We approach the pilot ready rooms, near a turbolift cluster, and are no longer alone.

At least a dozen pilots are in lively conversations behind the closed doors of the six ready rooms. Skywalker looks around us and considers how best to proceed. “What now?,” he whispers to me as the conversations continue around us. “What do you think?,” I reply as I lock my emerald eyes with Skywalker’s vivid blue eyes. I holster my blaster, flex my fingers, and the dark sense from my thoughts answers the question. Skywalker’s face shifts to dismay. I look away, settle my emotions, and focus on mentally preparing myself for combat.

“Just tell me which room has the fewest people in it and then get out of the way. I’ll do the rest.” “Wait a minute,” Skywalker says as he considers alternatives. I sense Skywalker’s emotions shifting as he thinks hard and tries to find a better way. Skywalker does not want me to kill any of the pilots because they are not actively a threat to us. If the pilots see us, they will alert the ship, then we could be killed or captured. However, unnecessary killing is not the Jedi way.

There are a number of Darkside abilities that bend a person to your will but they all come with a personal cost. Jedi use mind tricks but that is usually passive and do not last for long.  Skywalker looks at the doors to the rooms around us. “We’ll try this one,” he tells me and nods to a room. “But we’re not going to charge in fighting. I think I can suppress their curiosity enough for me to walk in, take the flight suits, and leave.”

“What if you can’t?,” I demand, worried about having to fight large amounts of the Chimera’s stormtroopers. “We’ll have lost whatever surprise we would have had.” “It’ll work,” Skywalker assures me. “get ready.” “Skywalker—,” I start. “Besides which, I doubt that even with surprise you can take out all three without any noise,” he added. “Can you?” My glare at Skywalker is intense with hard emerald eyes but I gesture for him to proceed.

Skywalker focuses his mind and heads for the door he indicated. It opens at Skywalker’s approach and he enters the ready room. A few minutes pass quietly. Skywalker emerges with three flight suits draped over his left arm  and the door slides closed behind him. “Well?,” I whisper. Skywalker nods, breathes out softly, and offers me a flight suit. I take it. “Go ahead and get into it. I want to try and hold off their curiosity for another couple of minutes.

“Until they’ve forgotten I was ever in there,” Skywalker tells me. I nod, unzip the flight suit, step into it, and pull up the fabric. It glides up my shins and thighs, fitting snuggly over my black trousers. “Handy trick, I must say,” I tell Skywalker, as I sweep up my red-gold hair, smooth it back, and twist it into a tight, double spiral bun on the back of my head, and secure with a hair tie so I match the pilots.

I am impressed that Skywalker found a way to leave the pilots alive, we remain undetected, and we have the flight suits. I was never taught something like that by the Emperor. Thinking back there were various missions during my years as the Emperor’s Hand where that Force ability would have been helpful. “It worked this time, anyway,” Skywalker humbly agrees and hands the other two flight suits to me. He turns back, gathers the Force, and focuses on the pilot’s room he just came from.

I sense him maintaining his gentle persuasion on the minds of the pilots, fading the memory if him to myth, and Skywalker is forgotten as he completes the trick. Skywalker’s eyes widen a little as he eases back on the connection. We wait for a surge of emotion that shows they remember him but the pilots continue their relaxed conversations. Skywalker’s Force persuasion and power level made that successful.

I tuck my arms into my flight suit, zip it up, close the neck fasteners, toss the other two flight suits onto my left shoulder, and head down the corridor. At the turbolift cluster, I summon one for us. The lift arrives, I get in, tell it to wait, and started keying in commands for a complex travel route. Skywalker turns away from the ready room and I beckon for him to hurry, “Come on, come on. You can change on the way,” I say quietly.

“I hope no one comes aboard while I’m doing it,” Skywalker says quietly as he boards the turbolift. “Be a little hard to explain.” “No one’s coming aboard,” I assure Skywalker as the door closes and we begin to move. “I’ve keyed it for nonstop.” Handing one of the flight suits to Skywalker and lock my emerald eyes with his vivid blue eyes again. “You still want to do it this way?” “I don’t think that we’ve got any real choice,” he replies.

Skywalker listens to me, responds as equals, then looks down as he steps into the flight suit. He pulls the fabric up his legs, tucks in his Jedi robes tunic hem, slides in his arms, gets the fabric onto his shoulders, zips up the flight suit, and closes the neck fasteners. The flight suit is too tight on Skywalker’s shoulders and hips as it wraps over his black Jedi robes. Hopefully that detail will go unnoticed for our short visit.
