Sara Almosawi, 24, is a daughter of immigrants and, through one lens, an exemplar of the American dream. Her parents immigrated from Iraq and Indonesia, met in Alabama, and settled in Orlando, Fla. Her father drove a truck while her mother mostly worked restaurant jobs.
She landed at Cornell after the school offered her generous financial aid—a “golden ticket,” as she called it. Then came Oct. 7th during her first semester in upstate New York.
As at other universities, student protesters built an encampment. They expressed disbelief that mainstream Democrats hedged over whether to call Israel’s conduct in Gaza a “genocide.”
The Democratic Socialists of America, with a long record of pro-Palestenian activism, was a natural vessel for those who joined the protests.
Once a baby boomer relic, the far-left DSA now counts more than 120,000 members, about half of whom joined since late 2024, after Israel’s war in Gaza ignited campus protests nationwide and energized young recruits like Almosawi.
DSA national leaders like Almosawi scarcely hide their disdain for a Democratic Party they view less as a partner than a hostile takeover target.
“Ultimately, the strategy of the DSA has been to primary mainstream Democrats. And we’re going to continue to do that,” she said on a recent afternoon as she sat in a Yemeni coffeehouse in Brooklyn. “We’re gonna take it over. We’re done with this. They’re not meeting the American people where they are.”
By late 2024, Almosawi faced her own reckoning. Cornell suspended her for disrupting a career fair that included defense contractors. Despite her parents’ misgivings, she has spent the past year nurturing YDSA chapters around the country while serving on the DSA’s national political committee.
“My intention was to graduate. But this is the most important time for socialism in America since the 1920s,” she said. “The iron is hot. The moment is now.”
Once a fringe wing, the DSA movement is wielding surprising political power, capitalizing on popular discontent. Mainstream Democrats see a "fundamental threat."

text:
Remember the hospital ship that was supposed to leave the United States and head to Greenland?  Everyone memory holed it.

What's really in Greenland?

In late February 2026, President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the U.S. would send a “great hospital boat” (referring to one of the Navy’s two hospital ships, USNS Mercy or USNS Comfort) to Greenland to provide care, stating it was “on the way.” Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen publicly rejected the unsolicited offer, noting the territory has its own free public healthcare system and that no such assistance had been requested.

At the time of the announcement, both USNS Mercy and USNS Comfort were undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in Mobile, Alabama. Practical barriers also existed for any Arctic deployment in late winter, including sea ice, the ships’ lack of ice-strengthened hulls, limited icebreaker support, and insufficient port depths for their drafts.

USNS Mercy departed Alabama around February 24, 2026. Tracking and reports showed it headed south through the Gulf of Mexico toward the Panama Canal (not northward toward Greenland), then north along the U.S. West Coast. It arrived at Vigor’s shipyard in Portland, Oregon, on or about March 19, 2026, for a planned overhaul/drydocking—confirming the movement was a repositioning for maintenance rather than a Greenland mission.

USNS Comfort remained in Alabama. No credible reports indicate either hospital ship traveled to or arrived in Greenland. The episode generated significant media and diplomatic attention amid broader U.S.-Greenland/Denmark tensions, but the ship never made the voyage.

FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED AFTER SELLING TICKETS TO THE SUNSET FROM A PARKING GARAGE ROOF

SARASOTA, FL — Perry Nash, 47, was arrested after setting up a folding table on the roof of a public parking garage and charging tourists $15 each for "premium sunset viewing access," despite the roof being freely accessible to the public at all times.

Nash reportedly wore a lanyard reading "SUNSET STAFF" and greeted arriving tourists as though checking them into an event
He allegedly set up folding chairs in rows, charging an extra $5 for "reserved seating" closest to the railing
Witnesses say he sold at least 30 tickets over two evenings before garage security intervened
He reportedly told confused tourists that "the view doesn't manage itself" when asked what exactly they were paying for
Investigators found a handwritten "capacity chart" limiting attendance to "protect the experience," despite the roof having no actual capacity restriction
Nash allegedly offered a full refund policy "in case of clouds," which he had never once honored, according to two customers

Tourists reportedly didn't seem to mind, with one saying "the sunset was genuinely beautiful, so honestly, worth it, scam or not."

"Twenty years in garage security and I've dealt with unauthorized valet operations, unlicensed food carts, I have never dealt with someone selling tickets to a free public sunset," said garage security supervisor Todd Ainsworth, 20 years with the property.

The folding chairs were confiscated, though the sunset, notably, remained free.

Dynamic in-road charging (charging while driving) has US pilots: Purdue/Indiana demonstrated 190 kW to a heavy truck at highway speed; Florida is targeting a 200 kW electrified roadway segment around 2027. These are test stretches, not a national network.eacf2b
Purdue
Room-to-warehouse RF wireless power (Energous PowerBridge and similar) is commercially deploying for IoT sensors, inventory tracking, and retail/warehouse use. FCC-certified transmitters are going into thousands of US sites, but this powers low-wattage devices over meters, not homes or the grid.8fd106
Investing
Room-scale infrared systems (Wi-Charge) recently shut down after 14 years, showing the difficulty of turning lab demos into a durable consumer business.4ba743
Invidis
Longer-range and “free energy” style systems
Kilometer-scale power beaming works in demos:
DARPA’s POWER program beamed ~800 W over 8.6 km with a laser (2025 record). Efficiency at the receiver was around 20%.febcae
https://t.co/MeAikveOfK
Microwave systems (Emrod and others) have shown tight beams with high collection efficiency over tens of meters to a few km in controlled tests, with end-to-end efficiency currently in the mid-30% range and targets to improve. These are aimed first at remote sites, islands, or military use rather than replacing US transmission lines.e7359e
Emrod
Space-based solar power (collect in orbit, beam to Earth) is the closest analog to the “universal abundance” idea. US activity is real and accelerating:
Caltech flew a demonstrator in 2023.
Startups such as Overview Energy (Virginia) have shown power beaming from a moving platform and are targeting a 2028 LEO demo plus first megawatt-class commercial delivery around 2030, including a Meta datacenter partnership
Pv-magazine-usa
The Defense Innovation Unit is soliciting commercial space-to-space and space-to-ground beaming prototypes, with an operational capability goal of FY2030.04d6ce
Meritalk
First useful (megawatt-scale) space-to-ground links are therefore plausibly late this decade or early 2030s. Gigawatt-scale systems that could matter to the national grid are farther out—mid-to-late 2030s at the earliest, assuming costs, launch cadence, safety, and FCC/spectrum rules all cooperate. End-to-end efficiency, atmospheric losses, and the cost of huge rectennas remain the main engineering and economic hurdles
Cell
Realistic US timeline
Next 2–5 years: More wireless EV pads, more in-road pilots, continued IoT/enterprise RF deployments, and military/drone power-beaming tests.
Around 2030: First orbital-to-ground megawatt demonstrations and possible niche commercial space power; limited terrestrial beaming for remote or high-value sites.
2030s and beyond: Broader but still selective use. A nationwide wireless grid that replaces wired transmission and delivers “universal abundance” to every home is not on a years-not-decades path. Wired renewables + storage + transmission upgrades remain far cheaper and more efficient for most US electricity.
The physics works. The engineering is progressing faster than it was a decade ago. Turning it into cheap, ubiquitous, safe power for the whole country is still a multi-decade infrastructure and economics problem, not a near-term switch.

text:
The man at the blackboard is Andrew Lo, the MIT Sloan professor who runs the Laboratory for Financial Engineering, and in these 80 minutes he explains why 4 companies' stock prices solved the Challenger disaster in 6 hours while the presidential commission needed 132 days.

This is Session 18 of 15.401, Finance Theory I, filmed at MIT in the fall of 2008. The first half is capital budgeting: the 4 rules companies use to decide whether a project is worth doing, 3 of which are wrong. The second half is market efficiency, and Lo opens it with a chart of 4 stock tickers on January 28, 1986. MIT charges $32,155 a term to sit in that room. The video costs $0. Millions have clicked it. Almost nobody reaches minute 60.

The Challenger lifted off at 11:38 AM and broke apart 73 seconds later. 4 contractors built the shuttle - Lockheed, Martin Marietta, Rockwell International, Morton Thiokol. The wire story crossed at 12:17 PM and named none of them. All 4 stocks fell together. Then they split. By 1 PM, Morton Thiokol was falling alone, deeper than the other 3, and it kept falling until trading in it was halted for the day. On June 9, 1986, the Rogers Commission published the cause: an O-ring in the Morton Thiokol booster, brittle in the Florida cold. 132 days. The tape had it in under 6 hours. Nobody leaked, nobody knew, and the price knew anyway. "This is the wisdom of crowds," Lo says. "This is why, when you look at market prices, you should look at them with a certain degree of awe and respect."

The hour before that chart is the part about your money, not NASA's. Payback period asks how fast you get your cash back, and over 80% of firms still run it, even though it ignores every dollar earned after the payback date and every ounce of risk taken to get there. Lo does not pretend the reason is technical: "Career risk is probably the most important risk from the typical perspective of the decision maker." Managers pick projects that pay back before their next review, not projects that pay.

The other two failures are quieter. IRR is used by 65% of firms, and the moment your cash flows change sign twice - a renovation, a second round of capex, a lease that turns negative in year 7 - it hands you 2 different answers and no way to choose between them. The profitability index ranks by ratio, so 300% on $1,000 outranks 40% on $1M, and scale simply disappears from the decision. That is how a company gets rich on paper and poor in cash.

Which leaves one rule. "NPV is always the right thing to do." Discount every future dollar back to today, subtract what you pay now, keep it if the number is positive. It is the same arithmetic whether the project is a factory, a solar install on your roof, a refinance at a different rate, or a job offer where 40% of the pay arrives as equity in year 4. Every quant desk pays entry-level analysts six figures to run it. Every advisor charges 1% a year to run it while you are not looking.

The math is free. The 80 minutes are the price.

text:
Farewell, Legend. 🥺❤️ Nimsdai Purja

There are no heroes in the mountains… yet Nimsdai Purja will always be remembered as one.

Just a short while ago, Elite Exped Nimsdai’s own expedition company officially confirmed his passing. They also announced that all those who had been reported missing in the incident have tragically lost their lives.

On the morning of June 30, a massive avalanche struck Broad Peak (8,051 m), the world’s 12th-highest mountain, leaving ten climbers missing. Among them was legendary mountaineer Nimsdai Purja, who reportedly fell nearly 800 metres during the avalanche.

In the world of high-altitude mountaineering, two names stand above the rest: Reinhold Messner and Nimsdai Purja.

Nimsdai rose to global fame in 2019 through Project Possible. Coming from a humble background, he became one of the most celebrated figures in mountaineering.

For decades, many Nepalese climbers were recognised mainly as Sherpas or high-altitude porters. Nimsdai changed that narrative by building his own world-class expedition company, Elite Exped, and turning Nimsdai into a globally respected brand.

From 2019 onwards, he continuously pushed the limits of human endurance. Many believe his impact on modern mountaineering rivals—even surpasses—that of Reinhold Messner.

Yet, as mountaineers often say, the high mountains offer countless ways to die. The mountains have no heroes.

Who was Nimsdai Purja?

Reached the summits of 8,000-metre peaks 57 times—the highest number ever recorded.
Completed 29 ascents of 8,000-metre peaks without supplemental oxygen, another world record.
Set a world record in 2019 by climbing all 14 of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks in just 6 months and 6 days during Project Possible, later featured in a Netflix documentary.
Led the team that achieved the first-ever winter ascent of K2, one of mountaineering’s greatest milestones.
Founder of Elite Exped, one of Nepal’s leading expedition companies.
Launched the Nimsdai line of high-altitude mountaineering equipment.
Founded the Nimsdai Skydiving company.
Took part in numerous high-altitude rescue missions, helping save many climbers on the world’s highest peaks.

Rest in peace, Nimsdai Purja. Your legacy will forever inspire generations of climbers around the world. 🏔️❤️

text:
*The Quiet Indoctrination* - Taught To Serve, not Think.

Samuel Chapman Armstrong founded Hampton Institute in Virginia in 1868. The school trained Black students in work, trades, and morals. It did not offer most of them a full academic path.

Booker T. Washington, Armstrong’s student, built Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881. In 1895 he stated the political bargain in the Atlanta Compromise speech. Accept segregation for now. Learn a trade. Cast down your bucket where you are.

John D. Rockefeller Sr. and John D. Rockefeller Jr. funded the General Education Board, founded in 1902. That board poured money into spreading Hampton and Tuskegee style industrial schooling across the American South.

The Phelps Stokes Fund, created from Caroline Phelps Stokes’s bequest, hired people like Thomas Jesse Jones to survey Negro education. It then sent the Phelps Stokes African Education Commissions in 1920 to 1921 and 1923 to 1924. They renamed the model adapted education and handed it to colonial governments.

Charles Templeman Loram, Natal inspector of Native education and later a member of the Union Native Affairs Commission, sat on that Phelps Stokes work. He pushed the American industrial model into South African Native education.

Apartheid later hardened the same logic as Bantu Education under Hendrik Verwoerd. Different schools for different destinies.

Democracy repealed the racial law. It did not fully repeal the machine. Crowded classrooms. One exam track. Most children sorted toward useful work instead of a full mind.

A child in a South African classroom today is not in Armstrong’s school. They are still inside his plan. Education fitted to the station already chosen for them, not to the person they could become.

text:
The High Priestess of West 86th Street
Margot Adler was born in Little Rock, Arkansas, on April 16, 1946, and spent almost none of her life there. The family moved to New York while she was small, and Manhattan is where she belongs in memory. She was the only grandchild of Alfred Adler, the Viennese psychiatrist who broke with Freud over the question of whether people are driven by sex or by the need to matter. Her father, Kurt Adler, carried on the practice. Her mother, Freyda, was a political organizer she later compared to Auntie Mame. Both parents were Jewish, neither was observant, and the household ran on argument, books, and the assumption that a child could have opinions.
She had them early. At eleven she was reading Greek myths and deciding, privately, that Artemis and Athena were more interesting than anything on offer in a synagogue or a church. That was not rebellion. It was taste. The rebellion came later and was political.

Berkeley, Mississippi, and the Sixties
Adler went to Berkeley in 1964 and arrived in time for the Free Speech Movement. She was on the steps of Sproul Hall when Mario Savio spoke and she was among the students arrested that December. The following summer she went to Mississippi to register Black voters, a nineteen-year-old from the Upper West Side knocking on doors in a state where three civil rights workers had been murdered the year before.
She would later call this period the heart of her life and say so in the title of her memoir, Heretic's Heart. What she meant was not nostalgia. She meant that the sixties gave her a template for the rest of her life: a belief that ecstasy and community were political facts, that a crowd singing could change something, and that institutions which denied this were lying about human beings.
She finished at Berkeley in 1968, took a master's in journalism at Columbia in 1970, and went to work at WBAI, the Pacifica station in New York. This was free-form radio at its most free-form. Adler hosted a late-night program and then a long-running show called Unstuck in Time, and she used the airwaves the way she used everything, as a place to think out loud with strangers.

The Witch of NPR
In the early seventies she did something that would define her public identity for four decades. She found the witches. Not the ones in fairy tales. The actual covens, small and scattered, meeting in apartments in the outer boroughs and living rooms in the suburbs, reconstructing a religion out of Gerald Gardner's books, Robert Graves, folklore, and improvisation. Adler was initiated into a Gardnerian coven in 1973. She never made a secret of it, which in 1973 was a considerably braver act than it sounds now.
Viking published Drawing Down the Moon in 1979. It remains the first serious survey of American Paganism written by a journalist who was also a participant, and the two roles never quite settled into comfort. She interviewed hundreds of people and let them speak. She reported on the movement's fractures, its egotists, its lineage fights, and its genuine spiritual seriousness without choosing between mockery and advocacy. The book has never gone out of print. Revised editions appeared in 1986, 1997, and 2006, each one thicker, each one a census of a religion that kept growing while the mainstream pretended it did not exist.
The same year the book appeared, she went to NPR. She stayed thirty-five years. She became New York bureau chief. Her voice, warm, low, slightly amused, was on Morning Edition and All Things Considered so often that millions of listeners who had never heard of Wicca knew Margot Adler as the woman who explained New York to the rest of the country. She covered the Central Park jogger case, the AIDS years, September 11 and its aftermath, and the small pleasures of the city with equal attention. She was a Nieman Fellow at Harvard in 1982. NPR knew about the witchcraft and mostly did not mind, which says something about NPR in those years and something more about how unthreatening she made it.

Love, Loss, and Vampires
She married John Gliedman in 1988, in Central Park, in a ceremony that involved a maypole and a great many friends and that she later described as a wedding and a rite at the same time. Their son Alex was born in 1990. John died in 2010 after a long illness, and in the grief that followed she did an unlikely thing. She read vampire novels. Hundreds of them. She thought about why a culture would produce so many stories about beings who cannot die and cannot stop feeding, and she wrote a short book about it, Vampires Are Us, which came out in 2014.
By then she was dying herself. Endometrial cancer, diagnosed in 2011, fought for three years with the practicality she brought to everything. She kept working. She kept broadcasting. She died in New York on July 28, 2014, at sixty-eight.

A City and a Tarot Deck
Sometime in the middle of the 1980s, a bike messenger named Giani Siri was riding through the city with a project in her head. Siri had come out of the Turner and Kirwan of Wexford scene, the arty punk rock band whose concerts doubled as Crowleyan ritual and whose followers called themselves Star Group One. She read tarot for strangers between sets. She had worked in a shelter for battered women and had come to think of the cards as a folk medicine older than psychology. And she had noticed, looking around at the crowd, that every figure in the Major Arcana was already standing in the room.
The idea arrived, she said, as a hallucinated neon sign reading The New York Tarot. She spent the next five years talking people into posing. No Photoshop. Everything done on film or in the darkroom. Quentin Crisp became Strength, in front of a library lion. Samuel Delany became the Hanged Man, upside down on playground monkey bars. Philippe Petit became the Fool. The Statue of Liberty became the Empress, the Unisphere the World, the Moondance Diner the Moon. Siri cast herself as the Queen of Swords. She self-published the deck in 1987 under the name Sirius Endeavors, ninety-odd sepia cards in an edition of around a thousand, and it never got much further than the shops that would take it on consignment. It is now one of the rarest photographic tarots ever made and, with Bea Nettles's Mountain Dream Tarot, one of the first.
For the High Priestess, there was only one candidate. The card is the tarot's image of hidden knowledge held by a woman who sits between two pillars and gives nothing away. In 1980s New York the person who had actually walked between those pillars, between the coven and the newsroom, between the sixties barricade and the public radio microphone, and who had written the book that explained the whole subterranean religion to outsiders, was Margot Adler. Siri did not have to invent a priestess. She had one on the Upper West Side with an NPR press pass.
What happened on the day the photograph was taken is not written down anywhere I can find. Siri has said that some of the sessions were themselves a form of ceremonial magic and that she chose sitters who could, for a moment, become the card. Whether Adler brought her own ritual objects, whether the shoot was in her apartment or somewhere Siri found, whether they laughed about it or took it seriously, or both, which would have been very like her, the record is silent. What survives is the card. Adler looks out from it the way she looked out from everything, as if she knows something and is deciding whether you are ready to hear it.
It is the right portrait. She spent her life as the person in the doorway, the one who could translate. The tarot has always understood that the Priestess is not the one who performs the mystery. She is the one who keeps it, and who decides who gets in.

text:
Tarik Skubal had exactly one Division I scholarship offer coming out of high school in Kingman, Arizona. Seattle University, a WAC school, saw him throw once at a fall showcase. He took it because it was the only one. Eleven years later he is the best pitcher alive and he just got traded to what might be the most talented roster in baseball history.

The path there is worth walking, because almost none of it looked like this.

He was a freshman All-American at Seattle U, then a National Player of the Week as a sophomore. Then Tommy John surgery took his entire 2017 season. Arizona drafted him in the 29th round that year anyway, as a flier on a hurt arm. He turned it down and went back to school to rehab. That is a 21-year-old betting on himself with nothing to fall back on.

He came back healthy in 2018, and the walks were still bad enough that he slid to the ninth round, 255th overall. Detroit took him. It remains the highest anyone from Seattle University has ever been drafted, and the reason he was available at all was the elbow.

Then it happened again. Flexor tendon surgery in 2022, the same elbow, six to nine months out. Two major arm operations before his 26th birthday.

Two years after that second surgery, he won the American League Cy Young. Then he won it again. In 2025 he posted a 2.21 ERA and had more double-digit strikeout games than anyone in baseball. The 255th pick with two rebuilt elbows became the best pitcher on earth.

Get exposure to copper - with a management team that deliver!!!

1. Company Introduction
Company: Trekor Metals Limited (TGB) is a premier North American pure-play copper growth company operating tier-1 assets in tier-1 mining jurisdictions (British Columbia, Canada & Arizona, USA).

Shareholders:
Insiders / Management: ~3.0%
Institutional Investors: ~18.0%–22.0% (key holders include Renaissance Technologies, Bank of America, Mackenzie Financial, Montrusco Bolton)
Retail Investors: ~75.0%–79.0%
Short Quote / Short Interest: ~2.50% of public float

From Past to Future: 
Transitioning from a single-asset legacy operator reliant on the Gibraltar open-pit mine into a multi-asset, low-cost North American growth engine driven by commercial production at Florence Copper and long-term development at Yellowhead.

Technology: 
Utilizing In-Situ Copper Recovery (ISCR) with Solvent Extraction/Electrowinning (SX-EW) at Florence Copper—delivering low surface disturbance, industry-leading lowest-quartile GHG emissions, and ultra-low C1 cash costs—paired with conventional open-pit crushing/flotation at Gibraltar.

2. Product Presentation and Current Developments
Products: High-purity LME Grade A copper cathode (Florence & Gibraltar) alongside copper concentrate and valuable molybdenum byproduct (Gibraltar).

Florence Copper (Arizona): SX-EW plant commenced operations in February 2026 with initial cathode harvests yielding 1.5M lbs Cu in Q1. Five active drill rigs are expanding the wellfield. 

Projected 2026 production: 30–35M lbs Cu cathode.Gibraltar Mine (BC): Strong performance in the Connector pit with Q1 production of 30.0M lbs Cu and 717k lbs Mo (head grade 0.25% Cu, recovery 83%). 

Full-year 2026 guidance: 110–115M lbs Cu.

3. Valuation Snapshot
Share Price: ~$6.77 USD
Shares Outstanding: 365.6M common shares
Market Cap: ~$2.48 Billion USD (~C$3.40B CAD)
Cash Balance: C$168.6M (~US$123.1M)
Total Debt (Excluding Lease Liabilities): C$735.6M (~US$536.9M) comprising US$500M 2030 Senior Secured Notes (C$686.4M) and Equipment Loans (C$49.2M).

Net Debt (Excluding Lease Liabilities): C$567.0M (~US$413.8M).

Enterprise Value (EV): ~$2.89 Billion USD (~C$3.97B CAD)

Q1 2026 Adjusted EBITDA: C$93.5M (~US$68.2M), implying an annualized run-rate exceeding C$374M prior to Florence full ramp-up.

4. Earnings Snapshot (Q1 2026 Financial Highlights)
Revenues: C$237.1M (+97% YoY), supported by an average realized copper price of US$5.74/lb.

Cash Flow from Operations: C$93.9M (+68% YoY).Adjusted Net Income: C$27.5M ($0.08 Adjusted EPS).

Gibraltar Total Operating Cost (C1): US$2.63/lb Cu, significantly reduced by a US$0.62/lb molybdenum byproduct credit (moly spot price ~$28.42/lb).

5. Peer Group Comparison
Peer Group: Capstone Copper, Hudbay Minerals, Ero Copper, Lundin Mining.Competitive Advantage: TGB offers 100% North American jurisdiction exposure (US & Canada), removing emerging-market regulatory and geopolitical risk. 

TGB trades at an attractive forward EV/EBITDA discount (~6.0x–7.0x 2026E) relative to pure-play peers (8.0x–10.0x), presenting significant re-rating potential as Florence cathode production accelerates.

6. Forecast 2027 and 2030 (EBITDA & EV/EBITDA Valuation)
2027 Forecast:
Production: Consolidated annual production reaches ~200M lbs Cu (Florence at full 85M lb capacity + Gibraltar at ~115M lbs).
EBITDA Projection: US$400M–$450M (assuming spot Cu US$5.50–$6.00/lb).
EV/EBITDA Valuation: Applying a 7.5x multiple yields an Enterprise Value of US$3.00B–$3.38B, target market cap ~$2.6B–$2.9B USD, implying a stock price target of $7.10–$8.00 USD.

2030 Forecast:
Production: Yellowhead online (+200M lbs Cu/yr average), bringing total annual group production to >380M lbs Cu.
EBITDA Projection: US$850M–$1.05B+.

EV/EBITDA Valuation: Re-rating toward Tier-1 producer multiple of 8.5x yields an Enterprise Value of US$7.2B–$8.9B, implying a stock price target of $16.00–$19.50 USD (>150%+ upside).

7. Acquisition Potential
TGB is an ideal M&A target for major mining houses (e.g., BHP, Rio Tinto, Freeport-McMoRan, Teck, Hudbay) desperately seeking long-life, low-carbon, US-based copper production. 

The Florence ISCR asset provides instant ESG-friendly volume with minimal surface footprint, making TGB a prime target as global copper deficits widen.

8. Catalyst / Milestones in the Next 6–12 Months
Florence Ramp-Up: Commercial wellfield expansion and SX-EW scale-up targeting full 85M lb annual run-rate.

Yellowhead Progress: Filing of the Detailed Project Description (designated as a priority major project by BC government).

De-leveraging: Prioritizing debt paydown using expanding operational cash flow to improve credit metrics and trigger potential capital returns (share buybacks).

Macro Tailwinds: Near-record spot copper prices (~$6.00/lb) driven by global supply cuts and AI datacenter/grid electrification demand.

9. Opportunities / Risks
Opportunities:
Structural copper supply deficit driving commodity prices higher.Substantial margin expansion as Florence ISCR lowers consolidated C1 cash costs into the lowest quartile.

Multi-billion dollar NPV unlocking at Yellowhead and Aley Niobium projects.

Risks:
Input cost inflation (diesel/explosives driven by geopolitical tensions).

Operational ramp-up risk during ISCR wellfield acidification and flow rate stabilization.Short-term price volatility (partially hedged via copper collars for Q2/Q3 2026).

10. Conclusion
Trekor Metals (TGB) stands out as one of the most compelling risk-adjusted growth stories in the mining sector. 

With Florence Copper coming online, robust Gibraltar cash flows, and zero debt maturities until 2030, TGB is at an operational inflection point poised for a major valuation re-rating.

text:
Christine Nyambura Muturi, who later changed her name to Christine Lewis once she landed in the United States, broke up with her husband, Bumula MP Jack Wamboka, amid public domestic disputes and moved into a path of scams and scandals on two continents.

She was born in the early 1980s in Kenya, Kikuyu. Little of her childhood is known. What is known begins with the work she did under the name Christine Lewis and the promises she made about nursing careers.

By 2023 and 2024 she was director of Westwick Institute Limited on UN Avenue in Gigiri, Nairobi. The school offered Certified Nursing Assistant courses and told students the certificates would open doors to nursing jobs abroad. Students paid. One paid 250,000 shillings. Others paid more. Police put the total at nearly two million shillings from at least seven people.

Westwick was not accredited by the Technical and Vocational Education and Training Authority. In May 2024 she stood in Kiambu Law Court on eight counts of obtaining money by false pretences and offering training without a licence. She pleaded not guilty. The magistrate released her on 300,000 shillings cash bail, ordered her passport surrendered, and told her to remain in Kenya.

At the time some still called her the wife of the Bumula MP; later called her his former wife. Their disputes were already public. In July 2024 she told reporters in Bungoma that the marriage had collapsed over domestic issues. She said Wamboka had dismissed her as his wife on the media, a statement she accepted.

She claimed she had been the main sponsor of menstrual-cup and school-lunch projects in Bumula that he launched under his name, projects she said cost nearly 20 million shillings and reached more than 9,000 learners. After the split she said she faced harassment and threats she blamed on people connected to him, including incidents she reported to police.

In the United States she used the name Christine Lewis. Court records list a 2015 arrest in Las Vegas for domestic battery. In January 2025 Los Angeles police arrested her as a fugitive from justice. By the time she applied for work in Arizona she was a convicted felon on supervised release.

In August 2025 she applied to Northern Arizona Hospice in Cottonwood. Her résumé claimed more than four years of hospice experience, including triage nursing at a Las Vegas hospital from 2019 to 2022, and a master’s degree in healthcare law and management from DeVry University. DeVry later said she had never enrolled.

She submitted a Colorado multi-state nursing licence number. The number was genuine. It belonged to a woman named Christine Lewis who was twenty-seven years older, lived in Colorado, and had never met her or authorised its use. The licence had been issued in 1980, four years before Muturi was born.

Northern Arizona Hospice was short-staffed and hired her. She went on patient visits with other nurses. On 15 August she made a solo visit. When the facility checked her credentials they saw the issue date. Confronted, she resigned the same day.

Within days she started work at Golden Rose Hospice in Mesa. Cottonwood police received a report. The Arizona Attorney General’s office confirmed she had never held a registered-nurse licence in any American state.

On 13 November 2025 an undercover agent from the Arizona Attorney General’s office sat across from her in a Tempe coffee shop, pretending to plan a new hospice. She wore scrubs and a stethoscope. She told him she still held a valid multi-state nursing licence.

Hours later agents arrested her outside her one-bedroom apartment in Mesa, near Crismon Road and Ray Road. The licence number belonged to a different woman. The patients she had treated were real.

She was charged with forgery, fraud schemes, practising nursing with a fraudulent licence, and computer tampering. Bail was denied. She remained in custody in Maricopa County.

The patients at both hospices were people in the final stages of illness.

text:
The same pattern appears much earlier in Egypt itself. Akhenaten elevated the Aten, attacked the cult of Amun, ordered divine names and images erased, changed royal art, and constructed a new capital at Akhetaten, the place where the Aten became effective. American Research Center in Egypt⁠ After his death, the abandoned gods returned. Tutankhaten became Tutankhamun. The old temples reopened. Akhetaten was deserted. Akhenaten’s monuments were dismantled and his name was attacked. The singular visible solar order attempted to suppress the plural depth of Egyptian religion; the suppressed field returned and swallowed the suppressor’s historical identity.

Seventeenth-century England offers another version. The monarchy was executed, the House of Lords abolished, theatres closed, festivals curtailed, and Christmas suppressed under the Puritan Commonwealth. Yet performance and festivity continued in displaced or clandestine forms. With the Restoration of 1660, monarchy, Anglican ritual, public theatre, court spectacle, seasonal festivity, and erotic comedy returned together. Parliament had closed the theatres in 1642; Restoration culture reopened them as major sites of public imagination. Cambridge history of theatre and prohibition⁠ The theatrical function had survived beneath the prohibition and returned with intensified visibility.

The Soviet case carries the pattern into industrial modernity. Bolshevism attacked Orthodoxy, sacred monarchy, inherited property, religious education, ritual time, and the ancestral village. Yet the new system immediately generated relics, martyrs, sacred texts, processions, icons, confessions, heresy trials, pilgrimages, and an embalmed founder. The religious function migrated into the party-state. When national survival was threatened during the Second World War, Stalin summoned older Russian historical and religious forms. In 1943, after decades of destruction, the state revived an official Orthodox hierarchy and turned surviving religious attachment into an instrument of wartime and imperial cohesion. Historian Kathryn David on the 1943 reversal⁠

Iran followed a related trajectory. Rapid modernization under the Shah displaced communities, weakened older authorities, concentrated power, and presented development as a linear escape from inherited life. The opposition did not finally organize itself through a more complete modernization program. It descended into the Shi’a archive of Karbala, martyrdom, injustice, sacred blood, the tyrant Yazid, and the redemptive suffering of Husayn. These symbols converted different social injuries into one field of action. Academic studies of the revolution show how mythic categories joined otherwise divided groups and made political events participatory reenactments of sacred history. University of Iowa study of Iranian revolutionary rhetoric⁠

China’s Cultural Revolution declared war on the Four Olds: old ideas, culture, customs, and habits. Temples, graves, lineages, books, teachers, inherited etiquette, and historical objects became targets. Yet the campaign itself produced a concentrated sacred order around Mao, revolutionary martyrs, the Little Red Book, confession, pilgrimage, icon, chant, and purification. The archaic structure returned inside the movement that claimed to abolish it. Later governments again drew openly upon heritage, Confucian ethics, civilizational continuity, ancestral history, and national rejuvenation as resources of legitimacy. Contemporary scholarship describes this deliberate use of traditional culture as cultural governance. Cambridge, ⁠Cultural Governance in Contemporary China⁠

text:
WAUKEE, Iowa – Waukee High School opened its 2026 football season with an embarrassing 42-7 home loss to Johnston on Friday night, a result that exposed just how lost the Warriors looked without head coach Gabe Bakker on the sideline. 

Bakker, who remains the program’s leader, was forced to sit out the opener after the district suspended him for the first two games following an OWI arrest last week. 

Court records show he registered a 0.23 blood-alcohol content, nearly three times the legal limit, after leaving a bar in Grimes. 

Assistant coach Matt Jeter stepped in, but the team offered almost no resistance as Johnston scored early and often, turning the contest into a one-sided affair by halftime.

The lopsided defeat raises fair questions about how the Waukee program handled the situation. 

Bakker has built a solid résumé across multiple Iowa schools and self-reported the incident while apologizing to his players, yet the district’s decision to sideline him for a quarter of the regular season left a talented roster completely unprepared for a quality opponent. 

Instead of supporting a coach who made a serious but isolated mistake and pleaded not guilty, the school’s rigid response appeared to prioritize optics over continuity. 

The result was a season-opening embarrassment that belonged more to the administration’s handling of the matter than to any single player on the field. 

Bakker’s absence was felt in every phase of the game, and Waukee paid the price.

text:
THE MARK WALTER CAPER

Insurance money, hidden  affiliations, and the $12.5 billion flip of a sports franchise. A decade of related-party finance built a sports empire. And now Federal  prosecutors are unwinding it.

BUILDING THE INSURANCE EMPIRE: 2011 to 2015

Guggenheim  Partners grew rapidly after the financial crisis by acquiring several  insurance companies. Annuity writers hold large pools of long-duration  assets, and whoever manages those assets earns lucrative fees on them,  often-times for decades. By the early 2010s the Guggenheim orbit  included Guggenheim Life and Annuity, and Mark Walter, Guggenheim’s  chief executive, separately controlled Delaware Life.

In 2011,  Guggenheim added EquiTrust Life Insurance Company. The Iowa Insurance  Commissioner approved an application from Sammons Enterprises and GPFT  Holdco, LLC, a Guggenheim vehicle, to acquire EquiTrust from FBL  Financial Group for $440 million. The approval order records two things.  First, Sammons was deemed a controlling person of EquiTrust because of  its large ownership stake in Guggenheim itself. The regulator accepted,  however, that Sammons would stay out of EquiTrust’s management.

Second,  the Guggenheim executive who testified in support of the acquisition  was Jeffrey Lange, a senior managing director with a substantial  quantitative background; he co-wrote a book on parimutuel finance and  holds derivatives-market patents.1Sammons is a  Dallas conglomerate that owns its own set of large insurers and was  therefore woven into the wider Guggenheim structure. Lange became  EquiTrust’s president and chief executive when the deal closed and the  story kicks off.2

In 2012, Walter led the  Guggenheim Baseball Management group that bought the Los Angeles Dodgers  for $2.15 billion. His partners included legendary basketball star  Magic Johnson. The partnership carries forward: in January 2014 Johnson  was announced as EquiTrust’s incoming controlling shareholder, and in  June 2015 Magic Johnson Enterprises closed the purchase of more than 60  percent of EquiTrust from Guggenheim.

Guggenheim gave up its equity in the insurer and stayed on as EquiTrust’s investment manager. That  arrangement, in which the equity changes hands and the asset management  contract stays put, comes up several times in subsequent years.3

STRATEGY 11: 2015 TO 2017

In  2014 Lange recruited Marcos Lopez de Prado, a prominent quantitative  researcher, and together they built Strategy 11, an algorithm that  recommended corporate bond trades. Beginning in 2015, three insurers  used it: Guggenheim Life, Delaware Life, and EquiTrust. At its peak the  program’s recommendations guided nearly $13 billion of insurance money,  according to an independent audit later commissioned by Guggenheim.4

The  unit that ran the program, Guggenheim Insurance Services, didn’t  register as an investment adviser to the insurers and didn’t charge them  fees. Guggenheim’s position was that the program only produced  recommendations and that officers at each insurer made every trading  decision themselves. Registration would have imposed a fiduciary duty to  avoid conflicts of interest and the SEC later examined whether this  would have been required.5

Data reviewed  by the agency showed that more than half of the trades Strategy 11  recommended were transactions between the three insurers themselves.  Cross-trades between affiliated investors are permitted under securities  rules but only at market prices. By early 2018, at least one executive  told the SEC that some of the trades appeared to have been priced above  what the bonds would have fetched on the open market.6

Some  concerns about these practices first surfaced internally. In 2017 Lopez  de Prado filed internal complaints about trades Lange had personally  executed for the insurers, specifically stock-index futures positions  placed after the 2016 election that would have profited from a market  decline. The market rallied instead. Guggenheim’s account of what  happened is that these were hedges designed by outside consultants.  Under either characterization, a Guggenheim executive held the  discretion to place directional derivatives positions with the money of  regulated insurance companies.

Here is where things started to  unravel. After making a reported purchase of an $11 million waterfront  home in Palm Beach in early May 2017 (according to county property  records) Lange died just weeks later.

Events following his death  moved quickly. In August 2017, executives at Guggenheim and the insurers  raised concerns about the cross-trades and put a stop to the practice.  In October 2017, EquiTrust’s investment staff recommended in writing  that the company stop using Strategy 11 altogether, citing among other  things, a lack of transparency in how the program selected bonds. In  January 2018, Lopez de Prado sued Guggenheim, Guggenheim Life, Delaware  Life and a slew of executives in federal court under the  whistleblower-retaliation provisions of Dodd-Frank. The suit was sealed,  then withdrawn after a settlement.

Later that month, an  audit by ACA Performance Services concluded that the strategy had  returned 5.9 percent annualized from mid-2015 through 2017 and had  beaten its benchmark. Guggenheim also retained an unnamed independent  expert who found that essentially all of the cross-trades had been  executed at or near the midpoint of the day’s bid-ask spread. When the  Wall Street Journal reported the SEC examination in February 2019,  Guggenheim’s explanation for the program’s shutdown was simple: Lange  had died. The insurer’s own staff, however, cited transparency reasons  four months after his death.7

3. THE NIRVANA ON THE CARVANA AFFAIR: 2016 TO 2019

While  Strategy 11 was running, the same insurer balance sheets were being  used for a different purpose. Carvana, the online used-car retailer  founded by Ernest Garcia II’s through DriveTime, funds itself by  originating subprime auto loans and selling them. Walter was an early  Carvana investor through a vehicle called CVAN Holdings, and in 2016  that funding channel absorbed 89 percent of the receivables Carvana  sold.8

From 2017, Carvana sold its  lowest-quality loans to a buyer it declined to identify. Transaction  documents and statutory filings identified the buyer from transfer  agreements as Sonoran Auto Receivables Trust 2017-1. The trust’s notice  address: 227 West Monroe Street, Suite 4800, Chicago. It was also the  address of Guggenheim’s Chicago office, of CVAN Holdings, and of  Franklin Monroe Administrative Services, the firm that keeps the books  of the Walter Family Foundation.

The named contact for the  trust was a managing director of a Guggenheim entity. Statutory  insurance filings showed Guggenheim Life, EquiTrust, and Paragon Life,  another Guggenheim-acquired insurer, holding equity in the Carvana  receivables trust or debt of its affiliate as of late 2018.9

Two  features of the arrangement stand out. The disclosed buyer of Carvana’s  better loans, Ally Financial, paid about 102 cents on the dollar for  paper with an average FICO around 680. For Carvana’s blended reported  gains to work, the undisclosed buyer had to be paying more than that for  loans in the mid-500s. In addition, twice at quarter end, in August and  December 2018, Carvana repurchased loans it had already sold and  immediately resold those identical loans to the same buyer at the same  price. In the process it collected fees of $4 million and $2.3 million  which flowed directly into its reported unit economics at earnings time.  Carvana told investors the buyer was unrelated to Carvana, Walter, CVAN  Holdings, Delaware Life, DriveTime, or Guggenheim. But it gave no  answer when asked whether the debt provider in the transaction was  related to Guggenheim.10

These concerns were  never publicly answered in detail, and Carvana went on to survive a  funding crisis in 2022 and recover. But hold that thought on Carvana.

TWO PROBES GO QUIETLY INTO THE NIGHT: FEBRUARY 2019

A  separate SEC investigation had been running since 2017, opened after an  employee complaint about Guggenheim’s asset-management business. The  SEC’s examiners flagged the firm’s disclosure of an investment in Atlas  Mara, then referred the matter to the enforcement division. They then  demanded documents about transactions involving ABS Capital, a Miami  firm run by former Guggenheim managers, and subpoenaed ABS itself. Among  the transactions questioned: an $85 million Malibu property that Walter  and ABS bought together, a loan ABS made to a fashion retailer, and two  other Southern California homes ABS purchased. On February 14, 2019,  Guggenheim announced that this specific investigation had been closed  with no enforcement action.11

Just eleven days  later the Wall Street Journal revealed the Strategy 11 examination. No  enforcement action in that matter was ever announced either. By this  point the internal complainant had been settled and Prado’s suit  withdrawn, the trades had been blessed by a retained pricing expert and a  performance audit, and the program itself was terminated. So by early  2019, the SEC had twice taken a swing at the Walter orbit, once at his  personal dealings with an intermediary firm and once at cross-trades  among his insurers. Both times they struck out.

ROOM FOR AGGRESSIVE EXPANSION: 2019 TO 2025

Over  the following six years the Walter empire grew considerably. Walter’s  TWG Global assembled holdings across sports and media. Here is the list:  the Dodgers, a stake in Chelsea FC through BlueCo, the Cadillac Formula  1 entry with General Motors, Andretti’s racing operations, the  Professional Bull Riders, and in capstone June 2025 an agreement to buy  the Buss family’s controlling stake in the Los Angeles Lakers at a  whopping $10 billion valuation. Dan Towriss ran both Group 1001, the  insurance holding company for Delaware Life and Clear Spring (the  renamed Guggenheim Life), as well as TWG’s motorsports arm, signing the  insurers’ financial statements while operating the racing teams.12

EquiTrust,  which launched this whole caper, changed hands again in 2025. Amistad  Financial, a firm led by Eric Holoman, bought the insurer with roughly  $3 billion of debt. Holoman had been EquiTrust’s chief executive since  at least 2019, and before that he and Magic Johnson had founded JLC  Infrastructure, a fund into which EquiTrust, Delaware Life and Clear  Spring placed roughly two-thirds of its capital within days of its 2017  launch. None of it was labeled as “affiliated” in statutory filings.  Fitch and S&P assigned EquiTrust negative outlooks on account of the  acquisition debt.13

Around the same time at  Sammons (in late 2024), the company converted its voting interest in  Guggenheim, roughly 46 percent of votes and 30 percent of the economics,  into non-voting economic shares.

After  the conversion, Guggenheim could be classified as unaffiliated, and the  related-party disclosures naming Guggenheim dropped out of Sammons’  2025 filings, even though Guggenheim continued to manage about 88  percent of the Sammons insurers’ portfolio for roughly $75 million a  year in fees.14

Throughout this  period, according to what has since emerged, the balance sheets of  Delaware Life and Clear Spring accumulated billions of dollars of  private-credit investments whose repayment depended on other parts of  the Walter empire. The loans reached the affiliated ventures through  intermediary firms. Press reporting names four: ABS Capital, the same  Miami firm from the 2017 investigation; Amistad Financial, Holoman’s  vehicle; Bradford Allen, a commercial real estate broker; and Hudson  Trading.

Reported destinations for the money include  American Media Productions, the vehicle for the Dodgers’ television  rights, whose notes sat on five Walter-connected insurers for a total of  about $1.45 billion as well as TWG’s bull-riding and media operations.  In statutory filings, Delaware Life reported its related-party  investments at $1.4 billion, about 3 percent of invested assets. Much of  the insurers’ bond book carried ratings from a single small agency,  Egan-Jones, and those ratings determine the capital charges the insurers  must hold.15

THE SURPRI(Z)E: 2026

A  whistleblower complaint about revenue accounting at Guggenheim Private  Investments reportedly set the current investigation in motion. In  February of this year, the U.S. Attorney’s office for the Southern  District of New York issued grand jury subpoenas to Delaware Life and  Clear Spring. The SEC opened a parallel investigation. The FBI executed  at least one search warrant on the asset-management side of the inquiry.

The central question? Whether the insurers concealed that  billions of dollars of their investments backed other parts of Walter’s  businesses, and whether Walter or his companies committed fraud by  hiding those connections while borrowing from the insurers. The Justice  Department has also gathered records on Egan-Jones’s ratings work;  Egan-Jones has stated that it is neither a subject nor a target.16

On June 26, 2026, the insurers disclosed the subpoenas in their statutory filings and restated their numbers. Delaware Life’s related-party investments went from $1.4 billion to at least $17 billion. That figure is around 40 percent of invested assets, against roughly $4  billion of capital. Clear Spring’s went from under $4 million to $3.8  billion. Group 1001 described the prior figures as “errors” discovered  through an internal investigation. AM Best and S&P subsequently  moved the companies to negative outlook, with AM Best citing weaknesses  in internal controls over financial reporting. The insurers then  announced plans to shed roughly $6.5 to $8 billion of affiliated assets.17

It  didn’t take long for the market to react. Guggenheim’s $1.18 billion  term loan traded down from the mid-90s to about 73 cents on the dollar.  Guggenheim, with little sense of irony and presumably to reassure  creditors, said that affiliates might buy the loan in the open market.  Walter then reportedly pledged his roughly 20 percent stake in  Guggenheim as collateral for short-term borrowing at double-digit  yields.

Then Walter agrees to sell the Lakers to Josh  Kushner and Bob Iger for $12.5 billion. This just fourteen months after  buying in at a $10 billion valuation, with the sale reportedly driven by  the need to pay down loans sitting on the insurers’ books. Sammons  publicly distanced itself from the situation, saying it had been  divesting its Guggenheim interest for years, and its long-serving chief  executive announced his retirement. Guggenheim’s President said the firm  is fully cooperating and that the accounting at the investigated unit  was appropriate.18

ASSERTIONS VS. INFERENCES

So  what can we establish based on primary documents or multiple  independent reports? Walter-connected insurers have repeatedly funded  ventures connected to his constellation of companies, his partners, or  Guggenheim. They have also purchased each other’s bonds under Strategy  11, Carvana’s loan trust, the Dodgers’ television-rights vehicle, the  JLC fund of Johnson and Holoman, and the roughly $17 billion of  affiliate-contingent private credit now restated at Delaware Life. In  each case the connection was either undisclosed, denied, or reported at a  small fraction of its actual size until outside pressure forced  additional disclosure.

Where pricing was visible, it favored the  affiliate side: cross-trades were reported to the SEC as above market, a  hidden buyer payed more than Ally for lower-quality loans, and fees  generated through same-day repurchase and resale at quarter end.  Internal objections were raised at multiple stages over the years. Their  concerns were handled privately. EquiTrust’s staff recommendation were  contradicted by differing public explanations. And the Lopez de Prado’s  suit was sealed and settled. The fact remains that both the 2017 and  2026 investigations each originated with an employee complaints.

The  inferences, which follow from the public record are these. The  structures appear very well crafted. The recurrence of the same  techniques across unrelated contexts over decades, always with the  affiliation one legal step away from the disclosure obligation; an  unregistered advisory unit, a trust with an administrative agent,  intermediary lending firms, a voting-to-non-voting conversion. It all  points to careful and deliberate structuring. But Group 1001’s  characterization of a twelve-fold understatement of related-party  exposure as an error is incredibly hard to believe.

The 2019  outcomes taught the organization that this approach could survive  regulatory scrutiny: the SEC had examined both Walter’s dealings with  ABS Capital and the insurer cross-trades, and both matters closed  without action. After that episode affiliate lending skyrocketed running  through ABS Capital again, among others.

At this stage it’s  patently obvious that the Lakers sale is a forced liquidity event.  Owners rarely sell a marquee asset of that kind within months of  acquiring control unless cash is urgently needed. And the reported  purpose, repaying loans on the insurers’ books, matches the exact  remediation measures the ratings agencies were demanding.

Finally,  the prior run-ins with the law now form a pattern that feeds into the  evidence pool. Prosecutors examining intent in 2026 can point to the  2017 SEC exam letters, the EquiTrust transparency email, the settled  whistleblower suit, and the Carvana-era denials as proof that the  organization understood exactly what related-party disclosure were  required and chose its structures with that understanding.

That’s  the difference between a reporting deficiency and a concealment case,  and it’s why the events of 2015 through 2019, which ended with no  finding at the time, now bear directly on how the current investigation  is likely to end.

THIS IS TOO COINCIDENTAL TO BE A COINCIDENCE

Maybe neither here nor there but we thought we would mention it. Thrive  Capital’s Carvana position was a distressed public-market trade that was  established in 2022 when the stock had collapsed. It grew as Carvana  recovered, reaching roughly 80 percent of Thrive’s reported 13F  portfolio by early 2025. Bloomberg reported in May 2025 that Thrive had  told its investors it gained $522 million on the trade, more than  quadrupling its money. The 13F record shows about 90 percent of the  position was sold in the June 2025 quarter, the same period as that  investor letter. 

The head of Thrive? Joshua Kushner. Yes the one who  bought the Lakers with Bob Iger from Mr. Walter.

To be fair the bulk exit predates public knowledge of the Walter investigation and  predates Walter closing his Lakers purchase, which makes it consistent  with profit-taking on an incredible trade.19

But  a residual position of roughly $70 million remained through the March  2026 quarter and was subsequently reduced to zero in the June 2026  quarter. The timing of that final sale is notable because it falls  inside the window in which three things were true: the SDNY subpoenas to  Walter’s insurers existed and remained nonpublic until the June 26  statutory filings and July press reports; Kushner was negotiating the  Lakers purchase from Walter, a transaction announced shortly thereafter;  and any due diligence on Walter’s finances would have surfaced the  insurers problems, since paying down loans on the insurers’ books was  the reason the Lakers were for sale.20

So again  three explanations are possible. The simplest is housekeeping: a  leftover tail of an already-harvested trade getting cleaned up, and $70  million is immaterial next to a $12.5 billion transaction. The second is  “conflict hygiene”: Carvana is the one public company with a documented  funding history running through the Walter orbit, via the Sonoran trust  and CVAN Holdings as an early investor. Any buyer preparing to transact  with Walter at that scale might reasonably want zero economic exposure  to Walter-adjacent names while negotiating with him (although in today’s  conflict rife world who knows).

The third explanation is that the  exit was informed by nonpublic knowledge of the investigation. Carvana  appears nowhere in the 2026 investigation, its Walter-orbit ties date to  2016 through 2019, and knowledge of Walter’s insurance troubles is of  doubtful materiality to Carvana’s stock. The small size of the residual  position further argues against a nefarious view. Furthermore such a  move would have been illegal so we know its not that.

But the  relevance here is to the broader fact pattern. The buyer who provided  Walter’s $12.5 billion liquidity event had made his firm’s most  profitable public-market trade in the company that Walter’s undisclosed  insurance channel once funded, exited that position completely in the  quarter the investigation gestated, and then completed the franchise  purchase.

Coincidence? I had the pleasure of being managed by  Yogi Berra before he and I both expired. He once famously said that its  too coincidental to be a coincidence…….of course he never really said  that….

But one thing is for sure. They really do establish that  the buyer’s circle was unusually well positioned to understand both  Carvana’s funding history and the reason Walter needed to sell. Now how  about that…

Watchdog Sounds Alarm on the Left’s Massive Foreign Money Pipeline
A new database traces more than $5 billion from foreign governments and charities into U.S. nonprofits since 2002, money that helps shape American politics through advocacy and…

By Francis Kapper
Contributing Writer

August 28, 2026

7 min read
Listen · 9 min
AMAC Radio

American US money bill of face value of 100 dollars old type close-up. Inverted illustration on a financial or banking theme. Federal Reserve: refinancing interest rate. Focus on the Fed stamp. Macro

A government watchdog group is urging lawmakers to crack down on foreign money flowing into U.S. nonprofits that influence American politics and public policy, according to letters exclusively obtained by the Daily Caller News Foundation.

Americans for Public Trust is sending letters to all 50 governors and officials on six congressional committees directing them to its newly launched https://t.co/XZH3QDNE9B database, which has catalogued a running total of more than $5 billion flowing from foreign governments, foreign nationals, and foreign charities into U.S.-based nonprofits with records dating back to 2002. The group is calling on state and federal officials to examine whether existing laws adequately prevent foreign actors from indirectly influencing political outcomes.

“The information is available. The threat is real,” Americans for Public Trust Executive Director Caitlin Sutherland wrote in the letters.

AMAC Magazine, free with membership
Federal law broadly prohibits foreign nationals from making contributions, donations, expenditures, and disbursements in connection with U.S. elections, but foreign money can still finance certain activities through tax-exempt organizations, advocacy groups, voter registration efforts, and other channels, according to Americans for Public Trust.

The Senate could next take up the Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act after the House approved the legislation in July. The bill would extend the federal prohibition on foreign-national contributions and donations to ballot initiatives and referenda.

Federal lobbying disclosures show that Common Cause, a nonpartisan government watchdog and democracy advocacy organization, and union powerhouse AFL-CIO have lobbied on the Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act, though the filings do not indicate whether the organizations supported or opposed the legislation. The groups didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The foreign money comes from a collection of overseas foundations and foreign-linked philanthropic networks. An earlier Americans for Public Trust analysis identified six major sources that it said had collectively directed more than $2.65 billion into U.S. advocacy groups.

Hansjörg Wyss is a Swiss billionaire who uses his massive wealth to fund liberal and progressive advocacy groups in the United States. Nonprofits associated with Wyss accounted for approximately $673 million, according to Americans for Public Trust.

His Wyss Foundation, a private charitable foundation, and Berger Action Fund, a nonprofit advocacy group, have directed more than $372 million into nonprofits associated with the Arabella Advisors network, a group of major liberal nonprofit funding vehicles, including nearly $305 million from Berger Action Fund to the Sixteen Thirty Fund, a liberal nonprofit dark money group, according to Americans for Public Trust’s database.

“Americans for Public Trust is a right-wing organization bought and paid for by Leonard Leo that has repeatedly targeted Sixteen Thirty Fund because of our support for progressive causes,” a Sixteen Thirty spokesperson told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “If the group were genuinely concerned about our campaign finance system, it would join us in supporting meaningful reforms that would increase transparency rather than selectively attacking organizations it ideologically opposes. We are proud of our work and operate in full compliance with the laws and regulations governing 501(c)(4) organizations. We strictly follow legal requirements regarding use of foreign funding.”

The Wyss Foundation and Berger Action Fund did not respond to a request for comment.

Join AMAC
Other climate activist groups, like British billionaire Christopher Hohn’s Children’s Investment Fund Foundation, accounted for about $638.2 million, according to Americans for Public Trust. The Children’s Investment Fund Foundation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Americans for Public Trust’s materials identify several major climate and environmental organizations among the largest recipients of foreign funding. The database lists the ClimateWorks Foundation, a U.S.-based public charity that connects philanthropic funders with climate change initiatives around the world, as receiving $582 million, according to the database.

ClimateWorks has distributed more than $2 billion to over 850 grantees in 50 countries since 2008, its website says. The organization did not respond to a request for comment.

Americans for Public Trust’s database also lists Energy Foundation China at $104 million from the U.K.-based Children’s Investment Fund Foundation and Quadrature Climate Foundation, and the Swiss-based Oak Foundation. The California-registered grantmaking charity has operated in China since 1999 and says it supports research, policy development and international cooperation aimed at transforming China’s energy sector and achieving greenhouse gas emissions neutrality.

Energy Foundation China did not respond to a request for comment.

The money has flowed into a mix of political advocacy groups and major environmental organizations.

The Sixteen Thirty Fund, a nonprofit advocacy organization that backs left-wing causes ranging from voting access and health care to climate policy and racial equity, received $305 million from the Berger Action Fund, according to Americans for Public Trust’s database.

The group also fiscally sponsors Chorus, a program that reportedly contacted dozens of Democrat-aligned social media influencers in June 2025 and offered participants up to $8,000 per month to promote left-wing messaging online. House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer launched an investigation into the program on Nov. 19, 2025, seeking records on its contracts, funding, and compliance practices amid concerns about the secrecy surrounding the payments.

The Berger Action Fund gave another $102 million to Fund for a Better Future, a social-welfare nonprofit that funds and fiscally sponsors projects involving elections, immigration, climate policy and other left-wing causes, according to the database.

The fund has also bankrolled Democrat-aligned advocacy, giving nearly $5.1 million to Building Back Together, which was founded by former Biden campaign staffers to promote the Biden administration’s agenda between 2021 and 2023, according to InfluenceWatch. It also gave $1 million to Planned Parenthood Action Fund, Planned Parenthood’s political and lobbying arm, in 2017, InfluenceWatch data shows.

Fund for a Better Future did not respond to a request for comment.

The funding also extended deep into the environmental advocacy world. Americans for Public Trust lists the Environmental Defense Fund, a global environmental nonprofit that uses scientific research, economic analysis, advocacy, and litigation to advance climate and energy policies, as receiving a total of $48 million from multiple donors. The Environmental Defense Fund did not respond to a request for comment.

The Natural Resources Defense Council, which employs lawyers, scientists and policy specialists to advocate and litigate on climate, energy, wildlife, and public health issues, received another $30 million, according to the database.

“NRDC is a U.S-based public interest organization that advocates for clean, American-made energy that can power the nation and address the climate crisis,” Natural Resources Defense Council spokesperson Mark Drajem told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “Our priorities and positions are set by our professional staff and our independent, U.S.-based board of trustees, and no one else. The funds highlighted in this database went to helping reduce pollution and protect wildlife in countries outside the United States.”

Some of those funding streams can be traced back to major overseas climate philanthropies.

Quadrature Climate Foundation, created by the founders of London-based hedge fund Quadrature Capital, has directed more than $568 million to U.S.-based organizations, according to the database. ClimateWorks alone received $148 million from Quadrature, including grants that Americans for Public Trust says were designated for efforts to accelerate electric-vehicle adoption and push financial regulators to address climate-related risks. Quadrature Capital did not respond to a request for comment.

At the state level, Americans for Public Trust pointed to Nebraska, Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio as states that have taken steps targeting foreign funding in ballot measure campaigns.

The congressional letter was addressed to the leadership of the House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Ways and Means committees, along with the Senate Judiciary, Rules and Administration, and Finance committees.

text:
Here is a story about how Walmart accidentally saved CVS from itself.

Arkansas got fed up with PBMs, the drug middlemen who sit between you and your medicine, inflating prices and steering patients toward the pharmacies they own. So in 2025, Arkansas did something no state had ever done. It passed a law, Act 624, banning any company that runs a PBM from also owning pharmacies in the state.

If you control the prices AND own the stores, you can starve every competitor and route all the money to yourself. So Arkansas said: pick one. You cannot be the referee and a player at the same time.

Watch how CVS responded. They did not offer to spin off the pharmacies. They did not even pretend to negotiate. Their answer was: fine, we will close all 23 of our Arkansas stores. Done. That tells you everything about where the real money is. The PBM is the crown jewel. The pharmacies are just a place to catch the money on its way home. Make them choose, and they will drop the drugstores without blinking.

BUT...Arkansas is Walmart country, and Walmart runs its pharmacy operation differently. So to avoid blowing up their hometown giant, lawmakers wrote a carve-out that effectively exempted Walmart while leaving out-of-state chains like CVS fully exposed.

And that carve-out is exactly what sank the whole law.

In July 2025, a federal judge blocked Act 624 with a preliminary injunction, ruling it likely violates the Constitution's Commerce Clause because it discriminates against out-of-state companies. In other words: by bending the law to protect Walmart, Arkansas handed CVS the precise legal argument it needed to kill it. Walmart didn't mean to rescue CVS. The exemption did it for them.

Arkansas had the right instinct. The conflict of interest is real, and other states are now moving on the same idea. But as long as the middleman keeps his seat in the middle, with the power to set prices and move the money, he will find a way to route it back to himself. Ownership rules are a speed bump, not a fix.

There is a simpler answer that needs no lawsuit and no legislature: don't use a middleman at all.

That is the entire point of us. No PBM, no spread, no smoke and mirrors. Just the real cost of your medication and a fair, transparent price.

The death toll from catastrophic flash floods in Nepal has risen to 675, and 2,500 people remain missing, including 90 Americans. The sound of helicopters looking for survivors. So far, more than 7,500 people have been located. Rescuers.. struggling to reach devastated communities along the Nepal-Tibet border. The scale of the disaster finally coming into view four days after so much water, ice and debris swept through Himalayan valleys. Hundreds of homes, cars and bridges were instantly destroyed. Emergency teams from around the world have descended on the area to help. U-N Spokesman Stephane Dujarric:: “Humanitarians are moving at speed to save lives with OCHA and partners from the World Health Organization, the World Food Program, and various assisting national authorities in Nepal to deliver urgent life saving support. ”
Families continue to wait for news about their relatives, and fears of further flooding have hampered rescue efforts.

37 people are dead and many more wounded after a Russian drone hit an ammunition warehouse near Kyiv. That sparked a massive explosion and fire. NewsNation's Laura Ingle:: “In a statement, the Ukrainian president Zelensky says a warehouse was struck followed by a detonation. Local military officials say at least 50 residential buildings were damaged in this attack, also causing a large fire spreading to other homes and a restaurant. All of it comes as the region experiences its 3rd day of air raids, choking the economy and disrupting daily life. ”
President Zelinsky said he would punish the individuals who allowed explosive materials storage so close to homes, which is illegal.

Nearly 590 pounds of cocaine was seized by the N-Y-P-D at a storage facility in Queens, New York.
Police say the drugs had a street value of about $10 million.
This week's seizure is the largest made by the N-Y-P-D in the past decade and the largest cocaine seizure in New York City in 20 years.
Three people were taken into custody and the investigation is still ongoing.

The U-S military boarded and later sank a boat on Friday that was allegedly used to refuel drug-trafficking boats in the eastern Pacific. Officials say the vessel was owned by the Los Choneros organization. Marines and sailors from the U-S-S San Antonio boarded the ship and removed people from the boat before destroying it with an airstrike. The last strike on an alleged drug boat in the Pacific Ocean came last Sunday, when two people were killed.

Tens of thousands of mourners have paid their respects to Norway's King Harald - who died at 89. People are laying flowers and condolence cards for the second day outside the royal palace in Oslo. King Harald's role in Norway was purely symbolic, though he was considered beloved.

That father, Nan Zhong, is now declaring a victory in court after a federal judge allowed a civil rights lawsuit alleging anti-Asian bias in college admissions to move forward.
The father and son filed federal lawsuits alleging a number of universities engaged in "racially discriminatory admissions practices that disadvantage highly qualified Asian-American applicants."

text:
Washington State 

State-Facilitated Retirement Plan for Private Sector Employees Through WA State Government 

Washington Saves Issues RFP for Program Administrator, RFI for Multi-State Partnerships

Washington’s State-facilitated retirement savings program is scheduled to open in July 2027.

August 28, 2026

The governing board of Washington Saves, Washington’s state-facilitated individual retirement account program, issued this week a request for proposals seeking a program administration provider, as well as a request for information about multi-state partnerships.

Washington Saves, set to debut in 2027, will provide access to a payroll-deducted retirement account for private sector employees whose employers do not already offer retirement plans. Qualifying employers will enroll eligible workers in the program at a default contribution rate between 3% and 7% of wages and will manage the deduction from their paychecks.

According to the RFP, the board seeks qualified bidders to provide program administration, investment management or “both as an integrated solution.” The program administrator’s services may include “program operations; IRA administration and recordkeeping; custodial and customer service; online platforms, reporting, compliance and communications support; and the design, management, monitoring and reporting of program investment options.”

Interested vendors can bid through Washington’s Electronic Business Solution portal until October 9.

The program administrator is not the first WA Saves position for which the board has sought bids: In August last year, the board announced its search for a consultant to support the program.

In addition, the RFI for partnerships is intended to explore “what a potential partnership with other state-facilitated retirement savings programs and their service providers could look like,” according to a Washington Saves’ release. Governance, program administration, technology investment management, customer service, reporting and other program operations are among the potential areas in which the board suggested it could partner with other states.

In 2024, Washington became the 19th state to enact legislation expanding retirement coverage. As of June 1, 22 states have enacted state-facilitated retirement savings programs. Of those 22, 17 are auto-IRA states, according to data from the Center for Retirement Initiatives at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy.

To date, eight of the 17 state auto-IRA programs have entered into partnership agreements, according to the Center for Retirement Initiatives. Colorado established the first partnership, the Colorado Partnership for a Dignified Retirement, in 2023. As of January 1, the partnership’s member states, in order of entrance, are Maine, Delaware, Vermont, Nevada and Minnesota.

The Hawaii Retirement Savings Board voted on February 10 to join the Multistate Alliance for Retirement Security, established in 2024 when Rhode Island’s RISavers program partnered with Connecticut’s MyCTSavings program. Hawaii’s program, enacted in 2022 and amended in 2025 to automatically enroll employees, is projected to launch later this year.  

State-facilitated retirement savings programs have accumulated more than $3.35 billion in assets as of July 31, according to the Center for Retirement Initiatives.
